speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the work of
the session has been proceeding fairly rapidly of late. We have exhausted most of the legislation on the order paper with the exception of supply. There are still one or two reports of committees to be received, with possibly one or two bills to be basedi thereon, and maybe another bill or two. I would suggest that on and after Monday of next week the house might begin its sittings in the mornings. I think this an appropriate time to bring the matter to the attention of the house. If there is no objection I would present the formal motion now; if it is desired to enter upon a discussion of the matter I should be glad to have it proceed immediately.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: personally, I would object to morning sittings for the reason that those of us who are trying to keep in touch with what is going on find it absolutely impossible to do justice to our work. I agree with what the right hon. the Prime Minister has just said that we are getting on very nicely and if we do not sit in the mornings it will only mean an extra two or three days, or we could possibly start at two o'clock in the afternoon. I would remind the house that it is particularly hard on the Hansard staff who have to sit here working while the house is in continuous session.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) who has just taken his seat, apparently mistook the thunderous applause which was given on the appearance of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) for approval of his Observations. In view of the fact that we have reached the point we have in connection with legislation and that the major part of the business which must engage our consideration during the balance of the session will be the estimates- I might say here that the government has been very derelict in not proceeding with them earlier in the session-I think we could get in two hours extra work in the morning without very much difficulty. It is impossible, strive as we may, to keep in touch with everything. I do my best but I realize that the government put it over on us very frequently and I agree with the hon. member for Battle River as to the necessity of having several supporters to watch what is going on. I am
quite sure my hon. friend will find it difficult to follow the intricacies of the operations of the mind of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), especially on the tariff, in this or in any other house. Some of my hon. friends have pointed out that it has not been customary to sit on Empire day. The other day I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister whether he expected the house would sit on that day and he said that was the intention. My memory was that the house did sit last year but I never trust my memory in a matter of that kind and I have not looked it up, but there seems to be an opinion on the part of many of our friends that as that day is being kept as a holiday by one-quarter of the world's population it might be well for [DOT] us to reconsider what our attitude should be in the premises.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Ever since I have been in the house we have always had towards the end of the session late sittings while at the early part of the session we have always had a number of holidays. This year we had quite a long Easter recess and now at the end of the session we are asked to hurry along with the result that much legislation will be ill considered. I join with what the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said, that we should have the twenty-fourth of May as a public holiday. We observed the holiday on May ninth, I believe some religious or church holiday, and if we observe a religious holiday I do not see why we should not observe Empire day. Not that I am an imperialist by any means; I join with my friend, David Kirkwood in the statement that he belonged to the British commonwealth of nations not because he was an imperialist but because he thought it was the greatest movement for peace which we had ever had.
These things are apparently arranged by the government as the private members of the house would seem to be just pawns in the game. I hope that the next session of the house will be so arranged that we will not have a number of holidays at the beginning of the session and then finally have to resort to morning and Wednesday evening sittings in the effort to rush things through.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I have been in this house long enough to realize that anything I say will have no effect, but nevertheless I am going to exercise the privilege of free speech. Personally, I have no objection to the house sitting in the mornings when the committee work is finished. Some of us who come from western Canada are
zm

particularly interested in the Canada Grain Act and have been attending one or two meetings daily of the agriculture committee. On one or two occasions this committee has sat three times in the one day and we find it impossible to keep in touch with the work which is going on in the house. maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for nine years I have been looking for an opportunity to support the right hon. the Prime Minister, and at last I have discovered something. I should like to put myself on record as being in favour of morning sittings. As the leader of the opposition has said, it is impossible to keep in touch with all the different committees anyhow. The hon. member who has just taken his seat pointed out that he had a committee meeting this afternoon. speechtext: As hon. members know, in matters of this kind the government is anxious to meet as nearly as may be possible the wishes of the house as a whole. With respect to Empire day may I say to my hon. friends that we did feel that probably the greatest service which could be rendered the empire by this parliament on that day would be to put good legislation upon the statutes. However, if there are hon. members who were counting on Empire day as an opportunity to visit their constituencies or to take part in Empire day celebrations of one kind or another, certainly it would be the wish of the administration not to disappoint them in that Darticular.

speechtext: Has the right hon. the Prime Minister considered that for thirty years, without exception, this House has kept Empire day?

I was not

Except once, when it came

If my hon.
friend says that such is the fact I will accept his word; I would be willing to accept his word on almost anything, particularly where it relates to Empire day. The government is quite prepared to have a motion presented immediately providing that the house shall not sit this year on Empire day. But might I suggest, seeing this is a matter of accommodation, that the two motions be put at the same time. We shall be losing a day out of this week if we give up Friday. We might as well make up that time next week by sitting in the mornings, and if that is agreeable, I would move:
That when this house adjourns on Thursday the 23rd of May, instant, it stand adjourned until Monday, the 27th of May; and that on and after May 27th instant until the end of the session, this house shall meet at eleven o'clock in the morning and that in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock, p.m., there shall also be an intermission every day from one to three o'clock p.m.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: May I suggest to the government and to the house that, instead of or even in addition to sitting in the morning, we sit until a reasonable hour at night. It is ridiculous to stop work just when we are getting into our stride. We are like a lot of school children being sent off to bed at eleven o'clock. This is absolutely out of proportion to our capacity for work or for happiness. My suggestion would satisfy those who wish to sit on committees in the morning and in the afternoon. We could make it a rule of the house that committees would not sit in the evening and that in the evening and until the early hours of the morning we proceed with the business of the country. In the few years that I have been in the house I have found that we get through more work in a much more intelligent manner after eleven o'clock than we do before. I would submit for the consideration of the house that at any rate we ought to be able to pass up our privilege of going to bed at eleven o'clock for a week or two until the end of the session.

The other day the Secretary of State laid on the table some correspondence with reference to the coat of arms for the province of Nova Scotia. maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES

speechtext: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you
leave the chair, I should like to call attention to a situation in this country which in the view of at least a great many citizens is far from satisfactory.
Early in the session I gave notice that I intended to move a resolution urging parliament to introduce legislation to prohibit clearance being granted to vessels carrying intoxicating liquor to United States ports. That resolution was not reached before private members' day was taken away. I should like very much to have been able to secure a recorded vote on a resolution of this kind.
I think it would have been of considerable advantage to the country at large if we could have been able to see just where members stood on this question. To-day I have not moved an amendment, simply because that would be regarded as a vote of lack of confidence in the government, and I should like, if possible, to see a free expression of opinion on the question itself and not have the discussion merely along party lines.
There has been considerable interest shown in this question, as is indicated by the large number of petitions from the various parts of the country that have been presented to this house. I am hoping that this discussion may afford an opportunity for those members who have presented their petitions-the member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) and others- to back up those petitions on the floor of the house.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Why single out the member
for South Essex?
^680	COMMONS
Export o) Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The member for
South Essex comes from a part of the country which is very vitally concerned in this question, and I have no doubt that, having received the congratulations of the Speaker he will be able to make a very eloquent appeal to the house. The government, although questioned in regard to this matter, has not given us its policy. Again and again throughout this session we have tried to arrive at the position the government intended to take, and I hope to-day that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) will state very clearly the policy of the government in this regard. The papers which were tabled last Thursday indicate nothing whatever except what might be called a "stand pat" policy. I regret to-day the absence of several members of the cooperating groups here-the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fan-sher), the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy)-all of whom were keenly interested in this question, and intended to take part in the debate.
Let me say that this is by no means a fight between prohibitionists on the one hand and, on the other, the advocates of so-called government control. I hope that from the very first we shall clear our minds of the idea that this is simply a question either of enforcing prohibition on this side of the line or assisting to enforce prohibition in the United States. It is a much more serious question than that of prohibition. It strikes at the root of organized1 government itself, and involves the most serious problems in international relations. First of all I would suggest that there is involved in this question the responsibility of government to parliament. You may remember the resolution which was passed by this house on June 18, 1926. I shall read only two or three paragraphs from the report of the special committee appointed to investigate the administration of the Department of Customs and Excise. Section 10 of that report reads:
The committee find that it is the common practice of the department to grant clearances to vessels wholly or partly laden with liquor for the united States, or allegedly bound for a toreign port, but admittedly sailing to "rum rows , and that false landing certificates have been produced to obtain cancellation of bonds given for foreign export of cargoes so cleared.
the committee further finds that a strong presumption is raised that some proportion of the liquor so shipped and cleared finds its way back into Canada for consumption. The committee, therefore, recommend that excise and sales tax be levied on all Canadian-made intoxicating liquors released from bond, no matter where they are carried and consumed, 
and that duty and sales tax be levied on all alcoholic liquors entering Canada, whether in bond or otherwise, irrespective of their ultimate destination.
Doubts have been cast upon the sufficiency of existing legislation to prohibit or authorize regulations prohibiting the illegal export of intoxicating liquors to the TJnited States. To the extent to which such legislation may be insufficient the committee recommends that it be amended. The committee further recommends that, as soon as possible, regulations be made to prohibit clearances being granted to vessels carrying liquor as cargo, sailing from a Canadian port to a United States port, such regulations to make an exception in favour of liquor being imported into the United States in accordance with the law's of that country.
I wish the house would recall the circumstances under which that resolution was passed. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) a little earlier in the session, had made, an impassioned appeal to the house to get rid of some of the evils connected with smuggling. The government was fighting for its very life. I confess that I was one of those who gave the government a chance for its life, and a number in this corner agreed in that policy. The government accepted the resolution. I doubt very much whether the session could have continued had the government not accepted it. The report was passed1 by the house. Now I take it that such a report, especially when passed under such circumstances, would be mandatory in character. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) often speaks of the necessity of maintaining responsible government in this country. May I ask him, to whom is the government responsible? Surely to the House of Commons itself; and' if the government is not responsible to the house then we have ceased to have responsible government. What have we to-day? To a very large extent, as I understand the situation, the cabinet is controlled by the Prime Minister; the party is very largely dominated by the wishes of the cabinet; and these groups undertake rather autocratically to carry through certain types of legislation with very little reference to the house at large. Do we call that responsible government?
It seems somewhat curious that the Prime Minister, who rather likes to boast that his grandfather helped to establish responsible government in this country, may be lending himself to a procedure which is undermining responsible government. I recall some words of Mr. Henry W. Nevinson, the great English war correspondent, in which he points out that at each stage in history we have to struggle to maintain those things which our forefathers won.
For freedom, we know, is a thing that we have to conquer afresh for ourselves every day

Export of Liquor-Air. Woodsworth
like love; and we are always losing freedom, just the same as we are losing love, because after each victory, we think we can settle down and enjoy it without further struggle. The battle of freedom is never done and the field never quiet.
I submit that we ought to have a very clear pronouncement to-day from the Prime Minister as to why he has disregarded a resolution passed by the house under those very peculiar circumstances. It is true that a royal commission was appointed; I myself, I think, was responsible for the suggestion as to the appointment of a commission. Though my own amendment was lost, the idea was incorporated into another amendment that carried.
I had thought that we were suggesting a constructive policy which might take this matter out of the heated atmosphere of party discussion, and that we might have an impartial tribunal which would guide us in deciding what was the best policy for the country to pursue. The commission was appointed and in due time reported. I quote a few paragraphs from its report;
The evidence adduced before us disclosed that -a great majority of such shipments never reached the named destination, and the inference was strong that the liquor comprised in such shipments had been smuggled into the United States. In many cases landing certificates were produced to customs that our investigation showed to be forged and fraudulent. In some oases the bonds were released, but in other cases the department was not satisfied, and the bonds are still outstanding. We have dealt with this aspect of the matter in our interim report No. 10.
For some time past an additional method has been adopted which is to export duty-paid liquor. The practice is to enter at customs the liquor as being for export to certain ports in the United States, but the liquor is never landed at a port recognized by the United States authorities, and is smuggled into that country in various places where there are no recognized ports or customs houses.
Many regulations have been framed and enacted for the purpose of meeting this method of smuggling, but they have proved ineffective.
We are convinced that the export houses are established in practically every case for the sole purpose of selling liquor to be smuggled into the United States and that they exist for no legitimate purpose whatever. Some of these export houses have customs bonds, and we would recommend that all these bonds be cancelled.
As all of the provinces of Canada have either assumed control over the sale of liquor or have prohibited it altogether, the principle of the Doherty Act should in our opinion be extended to prohibit the export from any *of these provinces by anyone other than the provincial governments or the manufacturer.
And this is the paragsaph to which I call special attention:
We also express our entire concurrence in the recommendation of the special committee of the House of Commons as contained in paragraph
10 of that committee's report. An effective method of carrying out the intent of the treaty referred to would be to prohibit clearances to vessels or vehicles of all kinds carrying a cargo of liquor to the United States, contrary to the laws of that country.
One would have expected action to be taken by the government but nothing whatever has been done. In addition to that, the Prime Minister himself gave a serious pledge to this country; on September 11 a full page advertisement appeared in the Toronto Globe under the heading "A pledge From the Liberal Leader." It said:
When returned to power I pledge myself to continue relentlessly the investigation of the customs service and to carry out without fear or favour the needed requirements.
What were the needed requirements? The committee of this house, after sitting for weeks, decided that one of the needed requirements was the prohibition of clearances, and their decision was confirmed by a royal commission appointed by the government. There is not the slightest doubt in the world as to what those requirements were; the Prime Minister stood solemnly pledged to carry out the needed requirements, yet nothing whatever has been done. I recall the high praise accorded by the Psalmist to the man who, when he made a pledge, carried it out notwithstanding the cost involved:
He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not .... He that doeth these things shall never be moved.
Nothing is said about what will happen to the man who does not do so. I would like to ask why the government has refused to act in this regard. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre is in his seat; I hope we shall have his support in this connection. We remember the work he did, for which I think we must give him due credit, as I did at the time; I think he should complete his work and help straighten out this international situation.
* Why has the government refused to take action? It may be because we are still going on the old principle of complete national sovereignty; sometimes I think perhaps the government has been unduly influenced by the " red-blooded " speeches of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mandon), who has told us again and again that we should maintain our national honour by doing this, that or the other thing. I think the time has come when we should realize that this old doctrine of complete national sovereignty is becoming obsolete. It used to be that each individual householder believed that his home was his castle and that he could do as he pleased

Export of Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth
without regard for his neighbours, but in our modern city communities we know that this doctrine cannot be maintained. I am curbed in a hundred ways by the desires and wishes of my neighbours who surround me. In the old days each city could do as it pleased, but to-day even the cities must conform to certain general regulations, because we are no longer living isolated lives. In my opinion the same thing is true to-day in international affairs; No one nation lives to itself. We are bound together by a hundred ties and we must have regard to the convenience and the welfare of other nations if we are to preserve our own national life and if we ourselves are to be treated decently. In the great street of the nations we are but one house, and we must remembeT that we must live in that street with the others.
If I might give a simple illustration, it sometimes occurs to me that our position is very similar to that of two old women who have adjacent back yards. The one old lady keeps hens and the other keeps a garden, and in one way or another the hens from the one back yard wander into the garden, and of course the old lady who keeps the garden is very indignant over it. She says to the other, "You keep your hens at home" and when the other old lady answers that she will let her hens run and scratch where they please, the first old lady replies, "If they come over here I will wring their necks." So the quarrel goes on, and at last the old lady owning the garden says, 'We must live as neighbours, I am going to erect a fence in order to try and keep your hens from my garden, but will you not help me do so? At least help me to stop the holes in the fence." The old lady owning the hens replies, "If you would only keep hens like I do there would be no trouble about your old garden; we would live as neighbours, without trouble." So the squabble goes on.
That is about the situation as between Canada and the United States; we have govern

ment control and they -have prohibition, and our government takes the position that as long as they have a different system from ours we cannot settle anything. We say, "If you put up your fence and make it tight enough nothing will happen", to which they reply that they cannot make it tight enough to keep out all the hens, so they ask our help. I believe that in ordinary law affecting community life we are beginning to recognize certain rights of neighbours. My little illustration indicates at least my position with regard to this international situation. I believe international neighborlin-ess is essential.
Mr. Woodsworth.]
There is a suspicion that powerful interests are behind the people who thus evade the law of the United States; hon. -members will recall the -reports of the royal commission, and from interim report No. 10 I have selected a few paragraphs. With regard to the Cosgrave Export Brewery Company Limited, the report stated:
An audit of the books of this company disloses the fact that certain moneys were deducted from the gross earnings of the company which were paid as contributions to compaign funds, in respect of certain plebiscites taken in the province of Ontario. There does not appear to be any justification for these deductions and as these were improper there would be due considerable arrears of income tax.
With regard to the Carling Export Brewery Company, the report stated:
In order to insure the success of these operations, it was necessary to procure customs seals, both of the United States and of Canada, and the necessary customs and shipping documents. According to the evidence, Low stated that he could procure these. . . . These cars had affixed United States and Canadian customs seals which had -been stolen or otherwise unlawfully procured and affixed to the cars, and customs and shipping documents that were forged or otherwise unlawfully procured.
With regard to Gooderham and Worts:
It was disclosed by an examination of the books of the company that large unvouehered payments were made, which were charged as part of the cost of operation, under various headings which did not show the real nature of the expenditures. Most of these payments were deducted from the profits before arriving at the amount upon which income tax was payable by the company to be government. The evidence disclosed that these payments were principally for political and propaganda purposes. In so far as contributed for federal political purposes, they were illegal and contrary to the provisions of section 10, chapter 46 of the Dominion Elections Act. . . .
With' regard to Hiram Walker and Sons Limited!:
The evidence also indicates that this company made large payments for which there were no proper vouchers and for purposes not recognized by the department as properly deductible for income tax purposes, and that the same were deducted from the profits of the company on the income tax returns made from year to year. The evidence suggests that the income tax returns of this company and the settlements made of the income tax should be reviewed.
With regard to Wiser's Distillery Company similar statements are made. Reporting the sittings of the royal commission at Montreal, The Toronto Telegram of June 14, 1927, stated:	[DOT]
James G. Lawrence, secretary-treasurer of the Consolidated Distillers, admitted that the sum of $380,608.59 was paid to both political parties between July, 1923, and the end of 1926.

Export of Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth
I do not accuse the right hon. the Prime Minister of receiving campaign funds directly from these great breweries and distilleries; I do not intend to imply that the members sitting on the opposite side of the house are in direct receipt of these amounts, but I do say that when it is a well-established fact that large sums of money have been used for political propaganda and for election purposes, it does at least leave some ground for the suspicion that in some way or another, in the underground workings of the party system, there are influences at work which are inimical to the public welfare. I have been informed upon very good authority that when one of the old parties starts a federal campaign it requires a minimum of 81,000,000; I think I have that on fair authority.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Shame, shame.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) may make light of that, but we have all been long enough in politics to know that these practices do exist.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The hon. member is
shamed with the small figure.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I said a minimum
of $1,000,000. It may be for the legitimate purposes of the party, but what I am getting at is this; large corporations are making enormous fortunes in this way and we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that by underground methods these corporations have tremendous power and may influence public sentiment through the party organization, through the newspapers and in other ways. The right hon. the Prime Minister and the government should very definitely clear themselves of all suspicion of participating in any way [DOT] or of being influenced in any way by organizations of this character.
Further the present practice encourages bootlegging. We have been told by government officials that bootlegging has been decreased to almost the vanishing point. Well, tell that to the marines, or perhaps I had better say " tell it in the maritimes; tell it on the Pacific coast." Personally I do not know much about the border between Ontario and the United States but I do not think that anyone who knows of the conditions there will say that smuggling has decreased to the vanishing point. I will frankly admit that the government has introduced some great reforms in the regulations and I want to give every credit to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) for the way in which he has carried out those reforms. There has been a reduction in the number of docks and an elimination of the abuse of the B-13 forms, and liquor is now being loaded in the presence
of a customs officer. I have no doubt that these reforms have done much good, but they have not been sufficient. In the report of the Liquor Control Board of Ontario dated October 31, 1928, Sir Henry Drayton, the chief commissioner, states:
It is hoped that substantial relief will he obtained through these reforms and that the short-circuiting which has so undoubtedly taken place, substantially reduced.
Sir Henry continues:
Bootlegging and short-circuiting will never really be stopped until proceedings are effectively taken against those Supplying liquor m the first instance.
According to the Toronto Globe on November 22, these regulations are not satisfactory to the Attorney General of Ontario. If we are committed to the government sale of liquor in this country we should supplement that by government manufacture and make the handling of liquors purely a government monopoly.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
We would save the
taxes too.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I think that is a
reasonable and constructive proposal which might be considered by the government. Let me repeat: If we are committed to government sale in most of the provinces of this country, I think the only logical thing for us to do is to go in for government manufacture; manufacture practically at cost because that would eliminate the bootlegger as he would have no particular reason to go into the business if the liquors were manufactured by the government and sold at as nearly cost as possible.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Sold abroad at cost?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I am not considering the sale abroad; I think that we will have enough to do at the present time to consider our policy with regard to Canada itself. In considering our foreign policy we might very well determine it on a somewhat different basis from that which now prevails under private manufacture.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Why manufacture at
all?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I do not intend to go into the question of why manufacture at all; I simply say that as we seem to be committed at the present time to government sale we should go right through with a public control policy and adopt government manufacture.
I charge that the present practice encourages lawlessness here in Canada. I should like to
2684	COMMONS
Export of Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth
read a few brief paragraphs from our daily-papers. The first is from the Toronto Globe of December 3, 1928, and is as follows:
There can be no mistaking the nature of the business itself or the men engaged in it. Official figures show that in the past trade year the Canadian customs cleared for United States points liquor valued at more than $25,000,000. This is not all. It is an open secret that most of the liquors ostensibly cleared for any of the four corners of the outside world are actually destined for consumption in the United States. This is big business-and it can be transacted only by those who daily risk their lives in evading our neighbour's police. It was inevitable, therefore, that the rum-running ranks should have been largely recruited from the gangs of gunmen and thugs who formerly inhabited the underworld of Chicago, Detroit and New York.
Is there any one so simple as to imagine that these gangsters are criminal only on their native side of the border and become good citizens the moment they cross or recross the invisible boundary? Such a hope is an impossibility. There are several hundreds of pages of evidence in the investigation of our customs scandal. A great many of them witness to the fact that these criminals are always criminals; that they are not in business for the fun of it; that they are not particular whence their profits come; that they just as readily smuggle narcotics, tobaccos or silks north as they smuggle liquor south; that their contempt for their own American government does not magically become admiration for the Canadian authority simply because it shelters them and abets them.
A particular case is mentioned in the London Free Press of December 3, 1928, as follows:
Last year J. D. Hanson, a native-born Canadian, was slain by a liquor enforcement officer for no discoverable reason. Hanson was not a bootlegger and did not even have any liquor in his possesion when shot down in cold blood. Children living in Sandwich had narrow escapes from death as long range bullets from guns of enforcement officers sped over the Detroit river. Motorists traversing the border cities along the water front were in danger of their lives. A state of siege every once in a while occurs on lake Erie off the Port Dover district, when it is not safe for law'-abiding citizens to venture out on the lake in their launches. They risk instant death or injury at the hands of the quick-trigger American liquor enforcement officials.
I need only mention the sensational articles which appeared in MacLean's Magazine of December I, December 15, 1928, and January 1, 1929. But I should like to quote a paragraph from a statement by Sir George Foster.
I read it in the Winnipeg Tribune of February 23 of this year. This is what he is reported as saying:
An organized band of rum-runners and smugglers who by the corruption of Canadian and United States officials, by outwitting the United States guardians of the law, and by the employment, if necessary, of gunmen and hired bandits, forced the forbidden borders of a friendly state and delivered therein to other 
organized bands of law-breakers, the goods banned by the laws of that country. By these methods and with such associates, Canadian brewers and distillers disposed of $27,000,000 worth of their wares in 1928, and pocketed their proportion of the illegal profits made by the venture.
Again:
The organization exists-it is skilled and experienced and absolutely unscrupulous; it is well armed with corruption funds and sawed-off shotguns, and shrinks not at the sight of blood. Why should the Canadian government give support and sustenance to so efficient and soulless an organization?
That question is being asked right across this country from coast to coast: Why should the Canadian government give support to such an organization as that? Let me quote this statement by Sir George Foster which, for me, is unanswerable:
The citizen of one nation who does not respect the law of another nation of equal civilization will not be likely to respect the law of his own, if it conflicts with his own personal self-interest.
I do not know that I can do better than reiterate that statement. It is all I want to say in the way of argument. The citizen of one nation who does not respect the law of another nation of equal civilization with his own will not be likely to respect the law of his own, if it conflicts with his own personal self-interest.
I want to suggest that the practice that now exists, encourages political corruption. The old brewing and distilling firms were well known. They had certain standards of public and private morality. They may have contributed and they did contribute to the campaign funds of at least one of the older parties and, I think, to both of them; some to one, some to the other, but the same corporation did not contribute to both. It was known to which party they contributed and they did so as any other corporation would. These new firms which have had such a mushroom growth and which have made such enormous profits, have the morality of bandits and pirates. They cheat even the government which protects them. I need not go into details but no later than May 16 I read this in the Toronto Star. I happened to be in Toronto on that date, but similar statements can be found in almost any newspaper. The article reads:
The Attorney General of Canada brought action against Hiram Walker and Son, distillers. to recover the amount of bonds totalling $107,000 and given by them on the export of 4.000 cases of whiskey to W. O. Watson, Guatemala, by way of Victoria.
Again:
Captain Nieholles swore that he sailed from Victoria, B.C., with sealed orders, which he

Export of Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth
opened after leaving port. These orders instructed him to be off a port on the west coast of Vancouver island and there to discharge 2,400 eases of whiskey. He swore he did so discharge the cargo to a steamer called the Pascawa, of Canadian register, and that 100 cases of Hiram Walker's was included in this discharge.
Continuing, witness swore that afterwards his orders were to proceed south to a point off the Faralon islands, off San Francisco, and that there he discharged the balance of the cargo, part to another steamer of Canadian register, the Chief Skujuid, and the balance to small boats, that arrived from the American shore.
Captain Nicholles swore he never went to Guatemala nor to Bonaventura, Colombia, that he did not know how landing certificates had been procured.
He swore that for the return voyage he required an outward bound report from the authorities at Bonaventura and a clean bill of health to present to the Canadian quarantine officials on return. These papers, he swore, were handed to him as his ship lay off San Francisco.
This sounds very much like the information that was given us some years ago by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). Instead of this having been cleaned up as we had a right to expect, we find that under the present practice these rotten conditions are being continued.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman
would give me time for a question. I am sure he does not, want to misrepresent anything. Can he give the date when this offence was committed?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
He will find that is one of
the old cases which is now being prosecuted.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am glad of the
correction. I did not look into the question of the date of the offence. The paper I am quoting from is of recent date. I quite admit that this case does not have any bearing upon or back up my argument at this point.
But to proceed, it seems to me that the refusal of our government to take action along this line constitutes an unfriendly act towards the United States. On June 6, 1924, Canada signed a treaty with the United States "for the suppression of smuggling operations along the international boundary between the Dominion of Canada and the United States and assisting in the arrest and prosecution of persons violating the narcotic laws of either government and for kindred purposes." Article 1 provides for the exchange of information concerning clearances of vessels, and article 2 provides for the elimination of the practice of granting fake clearances. Almost before the treaty was signed it was found that in practice it was altogether inadequate. So, as early at
least as October 6, 1925, we find the United States officials opening up negotiations with Canada-I have not the earliest letters, but a letter of that date refers to still earlier negotiations-to see whether Canada would not consent to legislation which would make the treaty effective. Under date of October 6, 1925, I find a communication from the United States authorities:
Suggesting, first, that-clearance be refused by the Dominion authorities to vessels carrying cargoes of liquor destined for the United States; second that a convention be concluded for the extradition between the United States and Canada of persons guilty of offences under the customs laws of either government, and, third, that a convention supplementary to that signed on June 6, 1924, be negotiated for the transportation of liquor to Telegraph Creek, British Columbia, via Stilcine river through Alaska.
Negotiations dragged on month after month. At last, on October 6, 1926, the Canadian government asked for a still further delay until after the royal commission had reported. It was pointed out by the Canadian government that:
The order in council instructs the commissioners "to continue and complete the said investigation into the Department of Customs and Excise and also to inquire into and report on the operations of the treaty made between the Dominion of Canada and the United States of America dated June 6, 1924, for the suppression of smuggling along the international boundary between the Dominion of. Canada and the United States of America and as to whether the said treaty is being carried out according to the declared intent thereof and as to whether any amendment to the said treaty is necessary or desirable to ensure the suppression of smuggling."
In view of the fact that the above inquiry has been initiated and that the reports and recommendations of the royal commission will be of great value in the discussion of the interpretation and possible amendment of the existing convention and collateral questions, the Canadian government is of opinion that it would be desirable to await its findings before setting a date for the proposed conference between representatives of Canada and the United States.
It is quite apparent from that letter and from the subsequent correspondence that the American people expected, and the Canadian government more or less conceded, that some revision of the treaty would be made. A preliminary conference was asked for by the United States and at last on January 8th, 9th and 10th of this year a conference on commercial smuggling was held. I should like to summarize a few of the important presentations made ait that conference, following the Canadian summary.
First of all the Canadian representatives made it clear that that conference had no real
2686	COMMONS
Export oj Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth
authority. It consisted of officials rather than of members of the government, and they had no authority to determine matters of policy and were called upon simply to bring out in discussion the implications of any proposals made.
The United States representatives showed that there was a growing importation of liquor from Canada. I quote from the summary:
According to Canadian official statistics the export of liquor to the United States for the year ended 31st March, 1928, amounted in duty-paid value to over $18,000,000. It was estimated that the importations from Canada formed the largest proportion of the supplies from outside.
I would urge that the amount of duty-paid liquor does not anything like cover the whole amount of liquor that was taken into the United States. Some of my official friends may be inclined to trust merely to the documents in this respect but some years ago I had some experience in waterfront work, and from inside knowledge I can testify that there is a good deal that goes on that is not found in the official documents.
Again, the American representatives stated:
Contrary to statements appearing in the press the United States officials were seriously attempting to solve the liquor smuggling problem. They had substantially succeeded in cutting off the smuggling of liquor from the high seas but had not been able to stop the flow across the Canadian border, particularly in the Detroit area.
Further:
The fact remained, however, that since the treaty went into effect between 1926 and 1928 the shipment of liquors to the United States, according to Canadian statistics, had increased.
With regard to the vessels that were operating they pointed out that the information as to clearances was frequently not sufficient to permit of identification. Then followed their proposal:
The proposal merely meant that each country should refuse to allow its instrumentalities to be used by persons engaged in breaking the laws of the other country. This remedy could be afforded by treaty amendment to the following effect, or by corresponding legislative or administrative action:
"The high contracting parties agree that clearances of shipments of merchandise by water, air or land from any of the ports of either country to a port of entrance of the other country shall be denied, if such shipments comprise articles the introduction of which is prohibited or restricted for whatever cause in the country to which such shipment is destined, provided, however, that such clearance shall not be denied on shipments of restricted merchandise when there has been complete compliance with the conditions or laws of both countries."
Quoting further from the summary:
It was made clear, however, in subsequent discussion that in addition to the renewal of

clearances the United States representatives considered it would be necessary, in order to cheek the flow, for the Canadian authorities to take steps to prevent the release from distilleries of duty-paid spirits for export to the United States.
Years ago the Liberal party negotiated a treaty for reciprocity between the United States and Canada. I am one of those who believe that that proposal should have been adopted. The failure to carry it into effect has been, I think, a tragedy for Canada from which we have not yet recovered. Here is another reciprocal treaty which has been proposed, a reasonable treaty, which the Liberal government so far has refused to consider. The Americans pointed out that other countries had done what Canada was refusing to do. Mexico and Cuba had taken action along these lines, and I understand, though I do not find this in the memorandum, that Japan has also done so. Norway refused to clear shipments of liquor to the United States, and not only that, but it penalized Norwegian vessels engaged in smuggling liquor into other countries. It was stated that Great Britain had taken action, but I believe that that was later questioned. In any case, Great Britain had gone so far as at least under certain circumstances to extend tSe three-mile limit to twelve miles. Quoting from the summary:
The United States delegation stated that it was their well considered opinion that nothing short of discontinuance of the existing practice of issuing clearances or other official documents permitting the legal exportation from Canada to the United States of goods which cannot be legally imported into the United States, would be of material assistance in dealing with the problem.
So they stated, very clearly indeed.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: What report is that?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am reading from the memorandum compiled by our own Canadian authorities as to what took place at the conference held in Ottawa between the United States and Canadian representatives in January of this year. I should like, however, to go just a little outside of that official memorandum to quote a couple of paragraphs direct from what was said by the American authorities. I read from the papers laid on the table:
Admiral Billard concluded his statement with a parable, based on the operation of Article II of the present treaty, of a man who asked for a clearance for his vessel with a cargo of liquor to a port in Cuba. The clearance was refused on the ground that the vessel would not be able to make the port specified, and there was. consequently, a suspicion that the liquor might be smuggled into the United States. The man thereupon asked for a clearance to Detroit rvith the same cargo, which was promptly granted, since all suspicion had been cleared away.

Export of Liquor-Mr. Woodsworth
Further, Admiral Billard said:
The treaty with Canada already concluded between the United States and Canada is entitled a Convention "To Suppress Smuggling" between the two countries. It seems to us, then, that Canada has already subscribed to the general policy, not only of reducing smuggling between the two countries, but of suppressing it. In other words, that we are not asking the Canadian government to adopt a new policy on this matter; we are asking them to take the policy they have already officially sanctioned, to suppress smuggling between the United States and Canada, and to supplement the existing treaty into -which they so willingly entered and which they have so thoroughly upheld-to supplement it by accomplishing that suppression of smuggling, to the suppression of which they have already indicated their official willingness.
The Canadian government since the conference has made a suggestion that it might be possible to meet the wishes of the Americans and to effect the desired reforms by permitting the American officials to be stationed at the docks on this side of the line. This, however, is the reply of the American authorities to the proposal. It is dated April 20, 1929. I read simply the essential parts:
In the above communication you were good enough to state that in order to cooperate with and further assist my government in the effective enforcement of its laws, the Canadian government was prepared to permit United States officers to be stationed on the Canadian side of the border, at ports of clearance to be determined, in order to enable the United States officials themselves to transmit immediately to the appropriate authorities in their country information concerning clearances of all vessels carrying liquor cargoes to the United States.
I now have the honour, under instructions of my government, to inform you that it is the view of its competent authorities that the proposed arrangement would not be a solution of the problem.
That letter is signed by William Phillips. Se here we arrive at the same point at which we started back in 1924-a deadlock, the United States asking that we would legislate in such a way as to enable them to carry out their laws, that we would not connive at the breaking of their laws, and we refusing to do what I think the world would consider to be a very neighbourly sort of act.
What will be the next move of the United States? Well, I cannot tell, but I found this in a recent despatch from Washington:
Someone here put it this way-"Canada has been asked to stop the rum-Tunners from her side before they start. Failing that, by far the biggest effort yet will be made to prevent them from finishing. If the Canadian government does not make shipment of liquor to the United States illegal, then the United States will talk to the Canadian distillers and their* rum-runnning agents in a language that they will understand."
If in this effort it becomes necessary to stop and examine everybody and everything that 78594-1U
crosses the border by auto, by boat, in railway cars; to stop and examine all express and freight shipments, there will be delay, discomfort, inconvenience and friction. It is to be hoped that this will not be necessary, but if the present temper on the United States side of the line persists, however reluctant the authorities may be to adopt such drastic measures, there is a feeling that whatever it is necessary to do will be done, but that rumrunning must and will be stopped.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
What paper is that
in?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: That is an article published in the Toronto Star of April 10 from a special correspondent at Washington.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Why don't they stop them?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Surely it is not
necessary to say that to-day, when the American representatives themselves have shown so clearly that under existing conditions it is next to impossible for them to do so. They ask our help, at least to a degree that we will not actively connive at this traffic, that we will pass legislation that will prevent clearances to rum-running vessels. But further than that, I find this statement, which was published, I think, in nearly all our papers. I read this in the Toronto Star of April 12:
"Only when it is apparent that a boat trying to escape search is faster than ours is gun fire to be used," an official said to-day. "Even then, under no circumstances, are boats to be followed into Canadian waters. We have warned the officers, in case the zeal of some of the younger men should run away with them in their desire to make a capture."
When the United States prohibition navy-
Mark the words.
-in this sector-
Mark also those words.
-is assembled within a few weeks there are to be twenty-nine "36 footers" capable of a speed of 45 miles an hour, and five "75 footers" capable of making 25 miles in heavier seas. The first twenty-nine will carry machine guns, and the larger submarine chaser type, will mount one pound guns in the bows.
In the whole history of prohibition enforcement along the Niagara river boundary, no fleet to equal this has ever been assembled by the United States to blockade Bridgeburg, Port Colborne, Port Maitland and Dunnville. This flotilla has to cover the shore line from the straits of Mackinaw to Sacketts harbour, opposite Kingston. In places of twenty-five "36 footers" last year, Commander Rasmussen has twenty-nine this season. Last year he had only 250 men, this year he has 300.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it strikes me that that is rather a serious situation to develop on our great lakes and boundary rivers. I was reading, with a great deal of interest, a speech made by the Prime Minister a few weeks

We are able to point to our unprotected frontier of over 3,000 miles, a frontier stretching from ocean to ocean across an entire continent, along the whole of which not a shot has been fired for over a hundred years.
That sifnply is not true, Mr. Speaker. And even although the orders to the United States officers may be that there is to be no passing into Canadian waters in pursuit of rum-running vessels, is it not inevitable that there will be exciting chases in the course of which there will be a rush to our side of the line? So narrow are these waters in some places that gun fire may endanger the lives of Canadian citizens, and should it unfortunately happen that any of our people are killed or wounded, it can readily be understand there will be passions aroused-well, it is hard to know whether those passions could be held in check. It may well be that the United States coastguards' in the I'm Alone case were in the wrong -I think they were-but are we justified in provoking such acts? That is another question and one we have to answer. Some of us have had to discipline children, either our own or somebody else's in school. Jack is told that he must not hit Mary. We say to him "Now, Jack, it is not nice for a boy to hit a little girl. You must not do it." Then one of these days there is a squabble, and poor Mary comes home crying and says "Jack hit me." I suppose we should then inflict condign punishment on Jack for having done it. Well, I confess that at times, in the case of such domestic troubles, I sympathize with Jack. Mary has been perhaps as tantalizing as girls know how to be-I am glad that the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Mac-

If the shoe were on the other foot I know that we should be indignant had the United States taken the position that we are taking.
We are maintaining, at enormous cost, an embassy in the United States to promote friendly relations. Are we going to maintain that embassy simply to try to protect international rum-runners, as in the I'm Alone case? I ask this question:	Why should we
shield a gang of outlaws, many of them American outlaws, whose business means gain to a small group of Canadian distillers and their parasites, but is not in the interests of the great mass of the people of Canada? I say this is not decent treatment of a friendly nation. All Canada is asked to do is to refuse to facilitate the operations of law-breakers. I have said earlier-and I do not intend to develop this point-that this trade as now carried on threatens the morality and peace of Canada itself; and that perhaps is even more important than the question of our international attitude. Perhaps I should not say that; I do not know whether it can be

Export of Liquor-Mr. Speakman
more important but at least it is of equal importance. And to recall the earlier part of my argument, since the government had such a clear mandate from this house, and since it had the report of the royal commission which the government itself appointed, it does seem that inaction on the part of the government constitutes a threat to the principle of responsible government itself.

speechtext:
It has become habitual in this house, so habitual in fact as to be almost a commonplace, for any member who rises to address the house on any subject to refer to that subject as being of such transcendent importance as to constrain him to take part ini the debate. While however this may have become habitual, I submit that the question before us is intrinsically and from the point of view of the Canadian public one of importance. It is, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has said, a subject of importance inasmuch as it involves our international relationships as well as the morality of our own people. As the hon. member was speaking, my mind went back a few days, and I thought of that treaty which was brought before the house having for its purpose the renunciation of war. That treaty was epoch-making in its importance; it was tremendous in its possibilities. It was based, not. upon law but upon the crystallized and articulate conscience of a people, and the measures for its enforcement lay not in legal action nor in legal penalties but in the indignation of an aroused people. And so with this. Many questions of importance in constitutional law are here involved, and there are many problems, staggering in their difficulty, in the way of administration. But these, notwithstanding their importance, fade to my mind inito comparative insignificance in the light of two other factors which arise-factors overshadowing the question of law or the question- of administrative detail, as the oak would overshadow-I was going to say the violet, but that comparison is not so apt-the shrubs and bushes at its roots. These questions may be divided into two; they are two great questions. First is the degree to which our action will affect international peace and international harmony as between two great nations, nations which for decades have prided themselves, and rightly so, on their cool-headed common sense and kindly consideration when dealing with their mutual problems. This matter before us is, I think, one which threatens the very purpose for which the treaty for the renunciation of war was brought forward.
I am not going to speak of connivance on the part of the government, for as I interpret the word "connivance" it implies a certain degree of approval; and I cannot believe that this government would or could view with any approval the actions of certain criminals -I speak of them as criminals, but perhaps I had better say certain men-in their own country. Moreover, I cannot imagine the present minister of the department (Mr. Euler) viewing the situation with approval.
I have known that minister as a private member and as the head of the department for eight years, and during those eight years my respect for him has grown as a man of courage, sincerity and character. I shall not therefore speak of connivance in that sense. But to the degree to which connivance may be interpreted as a knowledge of what is going on, without any effective steps being taken to curb the situation, I might possibly use the word. We have watched the effects of this trade, which is carried on legally in this', country although it is illegal in the country to the south of us; and we have seen that:, trade leading to conditions which we all deplore. As the hon. member for Winnipeg' North Centre has said, it is leading to the arming of people, a very small percentage of people it is true, in order to defend the laws of the United States against what they believe to be aggressive acts on the part of some of our nationals. You will note that I say aggressive acts on the part of some of our nationals, and I am not in the least confusing individual citizens of Canada with the government of Canada. That is a very different thing, but it has led to the arming of a -people and to the I'm Alone and other similar incidents. I believe that from the point of view of every right thinking man-and I believe every member of this chamber is a right thinking man-it may lead and has led to deplorable incidents.
I intend to speak very briefly on this matter; I wish simply to express my opinions and those of thousands of other citizens of this country, many of whom have communicated with me, and therefore I shall pass to the second phase of this issue, which was also touched upon by the hon. member who opened this discussion; I -refer to the morale of our young people. When you go to the frontiers of our country where this trade is principally carried on you will find men who have grown wealthy from this traffic; I am not sure that you will find women, but at all events you will find such men. The young people of Canada, who see these men and are associated with what is going on day after

Export oj Liquor-Mr. Speakman
day and who see so little effective action being taken to curb it, to my mind are subject to the great danger of setting up false ideas of right and wrong and of the heroic and the base. When they see men enriching themselves in this way; when they see these same men retain their standing as respectable and responsible citizens of the community; when they see that the actions of these men and the trade in which they are engaged apparently do not lower them in the eyes of the adult community, what kind of ideals will these boys and girls have? What will they think; what heroes will they set up? Then, to go into it further, right along our frontiers we find boys and girls and men and women becoming associated with the idea of violence and bloodshed, and I am afraid that we are coming to the point where familiarity does not necessarily breed contempt but where familiarity dulls the keen edge of their perception, wipes out the sense of right and wrong and takes away the right balance of mind.
Let me repeat that I am considering this as a moral rather than a legal issue. I am not qualified by either experience or knowledge to speak of the law; neither am I qualified to speak of the administrative difficulties, but I think I am capable of voicing here the opinions and the best common sense of some people at least whom I know in this country. It is their opinion that we are in <ianger of interjecting into our international relationship, into the international harmony and goodwill which is of such great importance, an element which will threaten if not destroy it, and that we are still more in danger of destroying all that is best in some of our people. I believe we are tearing down the bars which have protected what is best in mind and in conscience of these people who are now becoming accustomed to this traffic, and we are setting up in the place of statesmanship, of self sacrifice and of morality and goodwill an ideal of financial success without regard to how that wealth may be brought about. So it does seem to me, without being able to state definitely just what steps should be taken, that this parliament and this government should approach the subject seriously and with sincerity, and from the moral point of view as much as from the legal point of view. We should do what lies within our power to stop this practice.
I have heard it advanced as an argument against action being taken by our government that the United States is not very sincere or very desirous of seeing these laws enforced; we are told that they would rather

throw upon us the onus of that problem than assume it themselves. I can hardly accept _j,t statement without having very definite knowledge, but I do know that no matter how lax the officials in that country may be or how insincere in their attitude towards their own laws, it does not remove from Canadians the responsibility which rests upon us and for which we alone must account. So once more this parliament and this government have set the stamp of approval upon such repressive or preventive methods or measures as may be brought into force, they represent a people who are moral and peace loving; they are, I believe, individually and as a whole anxious to do the right thing both here and abroad, and in all earnestness and sincerity I appeal to the government and to the house to treat the subject on its merits and to see that at least Canada shall place herself beyond reproach.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, those of us who were here in 1926-26 will clearly recall that charges were made with regard to the administration of the Department of Customs and that a special committee was appointed to make a very careful study of the whole subject. In one regard at least that committee made a unanimous report to the House of Commons in June of that year, and on June 18 the house approved of the report. Among other things that report urged that:
.... regulations be made to prohibit clearances being granted to vessels carrying liquor as cargo, sailing from a Canadian port to a United States port	
That is a very simple recommendation which anyone can understand. Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, now the Prime Minister of Canada, gave earnest and hearty support to the investigation and to the report of the committee; he pledged himself and his party "to continue relentlessly the investigation of the customs service and to carry out without fear or favour the needed requirements." That pledge was given during the election campaign which followed the investigation by this committee.
Mr. King was returned to power and has done much to make the Customs department efficient. I for one wholly approve of the Prime Minister's selection of a minister for that department; I honestly believe I could not have done better had I picked him myself. During the first session of the next parliament a royal commission was appointed, which spent eleven months in finding out all the facts which were gathered from a very wide field, and that commission aproved of section 10 of

Export oj Liquor-Miss Macphail
the report of the special committee. I read part of this section a few moments ago, but now I would like to read the entire last paragraph:
Doubts have been east upon the sufficiency of existing legislation to prohibit or authorize regulations prohibting the illegal export of intoxicating liquors to the United States. To the extent to which such legislation may be insufficient the committee recommend that it be amended. The committee further recommend that, as soon as possible, regulations be made to prohibit clearances being granted to vessels carrying liquor as cargo, sailing from a Canadian port to a United States port, such regulations to make an exception in favour of liquor being imported into the United States in accordance with the laws of that.country.
Two bodies, a special parliamentary committee and a royal commission, studied this subject much more carefully than any individual could. They made a recommendation and parliament approved of that recommendation but has not carried it out. The next question which occurs to one's mind is: Why has not parliament carried out the recommendation which a committee of this house and a royal commission made to it?
I am concerned with how this matter affects the United States, but I am not going to discuss that phase just now. The speech made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) expresses exactly how I feel about it. There is no use in our talking about the peace of the world and in unanimously approving such things as the pact of Paris until we can deal effectively with an irritating and troublesome question which affects the peace of the world. It is nonsense to think that because the problem is irritating and troublesome to us we can escape the duty of putting a stop to the bootlegging of liquor into the United States of America. From my point of view the liquor business is a dirty business. I have never seen anything good come out of liquor and I have seen a great deal of evil arise from its use. It corrupts all those who touch it, whether they are individuals or groups of individuals. I have no use for the whole dirty business and the fact that we are allowing liquor to pour out of southern Ontario into the United States and are doing nothing effective to stop it is giving to the Canadian people the mentality and the ethics of bootleggers.
Very eminent gentlemen-I think one would call them eminent-are hunting for defences for our attitude. It is quite true that we are making money through the sale of liquor to the United States but what is the use of gaining even the whole world if we lose our national soul? How can we expect the young men and women, the boys and girls of this country to respect the laws of the land if
we do not respect the laws of. another country? Our example will mean more to them than our teaching; our acts will loom so large that they will not hear our words. From the standpoint of morality in this country we should do something about it, whether it be to stop the clearance of vessels or whatever it may be, and we should set about getting it done as rapidly as possible. Supposing we had a bad child in a community-we have been apt to say "bad boy" but I do not want to say that because there are bad girls as well as bad boys-and suppose that only one parent of that child was anxious that it. should be reformed and was doing everything to help the child to a better way of life. But some other neighbour in the community, knowing the will of the one parent, deliberately put evil in the path of the child. What would we think of that neighbour; what would we think of him as a community builder? We would have nothing but contempt for him, ahd that is almost the place we are in as a nation as between ourselves and the United States.

speechtext:
The question raised by the hon.
member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), so ably seconded by the eloquent member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-man), and supported by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), who has just spoken, is apparently one of considerable public interest, perhaps more so in recent years. But upon that question I think all members of the house will admit there is a very sharp division of opinion as to what the

Export oj Liquor-Mr. Euler
policy of the government should be. Undoubtedly there is a very strong body of public opinion which is opposed to the export of liquor from Canada to the United States. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated that that feeling is not confined to those of prohibition sentiments. I was rather inclined to think that such is the case, and 'that is not in any sense to be regarded as a criticism. It is equally true that there is just as strong and possibly a stronger body of public opinion which is entirely opposed to the suggestion that we should, in their words, assist in carrying out the laws of another country. For these reasons the government welcomes a very frank discussion of the whole question in all its bearings. Personally I am glad to have an opportunity of correcting some of the misconceptions that are apparently in the public mind to-day and to review as briefly as I can the situation as we find it. Essentially-and I think most members will agree with me-the situation is one that must almost inevitably arise where two adjacent countries deal with the liquor problem in two radically different ways. The one country, Canada, is "wet"-I think I may use that term-under a system of government control in seven out of the nine provinces: the other, the United States, has a drastic prohibitory law.
Something has been said with regard to liquor and' its evil effects. With some of the remarks I agree, but so far as the average individual is concerned, liquor is apparently a commodity in a class by itself. In my experience, laws with regard to liquor have never been regarded with the same respect as laws with regard to any other matter whatever. People who are otherwise quite respectable -and perhaps I should not use the word "otherwise"-people who are quite respectable, in this country in the past, and no doubt to-day in the United States, seem to have so little respect for prohibition laws that they will violate them apparently with no offence at all to their consciences. Liquor laws, dry or wet, always have had a strong minority, or possibly, even a majority opposed to them. I believe it is literally impossible for a wet country to lie adjacent to a so-called or ostensibly dry country without a flow of liquor proceeding from the wet to the dry. That, of course, is the basic reason to-day for the situation which we are now debating.
During the war Canada had a prohibitory law. The United States continued wet. They were not yet in the war. Liquor flowed freely at that time from the United States to Canada.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Very little.
