speechtext:
It is perhaps fair to say
that I have no recollection, and I think no one has any, that the United States, at a time when conditions were reversed, made any effort whatever to stop the exportation of liquor from one friendly nation to another friendly nation which was engaged in a great war. I am not sure that that is an argument, but in any disposition we may make of the question I believe we ought to consider the attitude of the United States itself in regard to this matter. To-day with Canada wet, and the United States ostensibly dry, the flow is from us to them.
I want to congratulate the members in that corner who have discussed the question from a very high moral plane and to assure them that I desire to discuss it solely on its merits. When I ray that, I wish for a moment to take exception to an inference apparently drawn by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he says that it is at least suspicious that no action is taken in the direction which he desires and that perhaps we may be influenced by money which would flow out of the coffers of the distillers and brewers into party funds. I am not sure whether it is worth while denying that, but if it is, so far as I am concerned I wish to issue an absolute denial. No better proof of the sincerity of that denial can be offered than the fact that in every case where action was recommended against brewers and distillers who had not paid their taxes, that action was proceeded with without any* exception whatsoever. We have collected from those brewers and distillers a good many million dollars, and expect to get some more.
Perhaps I might deal briefly with the subject in chronological order. As has been said, in 1924, a treaty was concluded with the United States for the suppression of smuggling. The chief obligation into which Canada entered was that we should report to the United States authorities whenever a clearance was granted by Canadian customs officials to liquor-laden boats bound for the United States. A good many other things were discussed, but those who are familiar with the treaty will agree that that was the outstanding obligation in it. May I say in passing that the United States government on several occasions has stated officially that the Canadian government, through the Department of National Revenue, has faithfully carried out the obligations embodied in that treaty. But the United States has not been satisfied with the provisions of the treaty. With that I have no particular fault to find. Indeed, before the treaty was
Export oj Liquor-Mr. Euler

made, the United States requested that there should be inserted in it a provision that mo clearances be granted to vessels of the kind mentioned, namely, vessels carrying liquor to United States shores. It was not so included in the treaty. We merely agreed to give notice of clearances that had been granted.
As has already been stated, in 1926 a request came from the United States government for a further conference with the Canadian authorities, their purpose being to persuade the Canadian government, if possible, to grant the very thing which they are again-now asking. That conference, held last January, was attended by certain officials of the United States government and the Canadian government. Suffice it to say that the outcome of the conference was merely this, that the Canadian officials expressed doubt as to the efficacy of the remedy proposed by the United States officials, and that the United States officials re-asserted their conviction that the only way in which the difficulty could be met was. by Canada passing such regulations or such laws as would prevent the export of liquor to the United States. I might say here, although I shall come to that point later, that merely to prohibit the granting of clearances will not remedy the situation at all. To make such a measure effective you would also have to forbid the release of liquor or beer from the distilleries and breweries.
I have spoken of the net result of the conference of last January. Following the conference, the officials made their reports to their respective governments. The report of the Canadian officials was received by the government some months ago. After some consideration by the government a communication was sent to the United States suggesting a proposal, which has already been described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that it was thought would be of assistance to the United States, namely to permit them to station their agents on Canadian docks from which liquor was being exported, so that they could observe and report to their own government and thereby stop the export to the United States, The United States authorities, in further correspondence, reverted to their former request and stated that the only thing that would serve their purpose would be for this government to stop the issue of clearances. There the matter stands to-day.
I should like, because I think it is of interest and will remove misapprehension in the minds of some hon. members and certainly of some people in this country, to describe what takes place in the exporting of liquor. In the first place it should be understood that liquor
(Mr. Euler.]
*manufactured and sold in Canada pays an excise tax of $9 a gallon. Liquor imported into Canada pays a duty of $10 a gallon-a little bit of protection, as some of my Conservative friends would say.

It all depends upon the country to which it is being exported. If the liquor is actually exported to the West Indies, if it actually goes there, the method is this:	The
liquor does not pay an excise tax as it leaves the distillery, but the shipper gives a bond issued by a reliable guarantee company for twice the amount of the excise tax. That bond is released and cancelled by the Department of National Revenue when the shipper brings back from the country to which the goods were shipped a bona fide landing certificate, showing that the goods were actually landed in that foreign country.
Some reference has been made to the fact that in the past a good many bogus landing certificates have been obtained and the bond released when the liquor was not actually landed in the foreign country to which it was destined. I want to assure the house that that practice has absolutely discontinued; that the bonds which are given are bona fide bonds, and that the landing certificates which we receive and upon the receipt of which we cancel the bonds are absolutely genuine; there is no doubt about that.
Liquor exported to the United States is in a different class in this way: It is apparent, of course, to every member that it is impossible for a vessel to obtain a landing certificate for liquor shipped to the United States, that country being under a prohibitory law. Therefore, in order to avoid any difficulty, the practice is for the distillers to pay the excise tax before the goods leave the distillery.

Mr. Speaker, I have only
forty minutes, and although I should be glad to answer any questions if my time were extended, there are certain things that I should like to say. In any case I cannot answer my hon. friend's question; that was before I took charge of the department.
When liquor is destined for the United States, the excise is paid and it is then just as legal to export that liquor as any other commodity-boots and shoes, furniture, iron and steel, or anything else that can legally be exported. So far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned, when the excise tax is paid, all its demands are satisfied and the liquor becomes exactly similar to any other commodity that might be manufactured in Canada. When these liquors are exported to the United States, however, it is necessary that the boat or conveyance carrying them to the United States obtain a clearance from the Canadian customs and fill out the necessary export papers. That is the whole procedure.
Most of the liquor that goes from Canada to the United States is shipped from what we may call the Windsor-Detroit front and the Lake Erie front. Some goes over the border from lake Ontario, and some from western Canada and from Quebec, but not so very much. Most of it goes out from the area I have mentioned in the province of Ontario, and some from the province of Quebec. In every case clearances and export entries are necessary under our law.
I should like to correct a few misconceptions that are current throughout the country. It has been stated that the government loses revenue by reason of the export of liquor to the United States. That is not the fact. Every bottle of liquor that leaves a distillery in Canada, no matter where it goes, pays the excise tax before it leaves the distillery unless it is bona fide destined for some foreign country where bona fide landing certificates can be obtained, and in that case the shipment is made under bond. It is no longer true, as some people believe, that clearances to small boats are issued from our lake ports to countries like Cuba or Mexico. That practice was discontinued even before I took charge of the department. No boat which it is quite evident cannot proceed to the destination designated in its papers can receive a clearance.
Reference was made to a clearance being refused to a boat at Bridgeburg going to Mexico because it was quite apparent that it could not proceed there, and a clearance being given when it was stated that the boat
would go to Detroit. I do not see anything very peculiar in that, because in the one case the master of that boat gave a false declaration, and in the other he did not. In the one case he was violating our customs law, in the other he was not. I think it will surprise the members of the house when I say that when these boats clear from Windsor, we will say, for Detroit, or from Bridgeburg for Buffalo, they go to Detroit and go to Buffalo. They clear for a definite destination. If we know that they are clearing for some destination to which they are not actually going, they are violating our law and a penalty is applied.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Do they present their
clearances to the port to which they go?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I do not suppose so. I am glad my hon. friend' mentioned that point; I might as well deal with it now. The boats which are smuggling liquor are not violating our law, 'because it is not smuggling while they are in Canada. But when they deliver liquor in the United States they are violating American law, and the boats that are carrying this 'liquor to the United) States are almost 100 per cent United States boats; they are not Canadian boats at all. Not only that, the men who are carrying the goods across are Americans practically 100 per cent, not Canadians. Here is a peculiarity in the respective laws of the two countries. In Canada every boat, no matter how small it is-and most of these goods are carried in small boats-must obtain clearance from a Canadian customs officer. In the United1 States-and these boats are owned in the United States, I should like the house to remember-boats under 5 tons need not obtain clearance, and need not report when they come back. In Canada they must obtain clearance when they leave and report when they come 'back. While the United States are asking that we discontinue clearances to these boats-their own boats manned by their own people-they do not demand clearances themselves from those very boats.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Are these boats not treated in exactly the same way as a boat carrying, we will say, a shipload of potatoes? Suppose an American boat came across here for a cargo of potatoes, she would get clearance and would be treated in exactly the same way as these rum boats?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, exactly the same. The difference is in the tonnage. In the United States they demand clearance of boats of five tons and over. But the anomaly is in this'

Export of Liquor-Mr. Euler
They now ask us to discontinue giving clearances to their own boats, which in most cases ore less than five tons. They themselves do not require clearances of those boats. I would respectfully suggest that they would have considerably more control over their own boats, manned by their own people, if they would enact a law that those boats, no matter how small, should be obliged to obtain clearances when they leave their shore and report when they come back, the same as we require in Canada. That would give them some control.

I do not think he should say "we" have.

It has been said, I think by the member for Winnipeg North Centre, that we have done absolutely nothing to assist the United States. I desire to cite some of the things we have done.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I thought I gave the government credit for having done something.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQTJOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Perhaps I am accusing the hon. member wrongfully, but I understood him to say that we had not done anything to assist the United States. The first thing we did was to agree to a treaty establishing the twelve-mile limit, which has at times involved considerable difficulty to Canadian boats. That
helped tremendously in stopping the importation of liquor from the Atlantic seaboard. We agreed to give information as to clearances and have faithfully carried out that agreement, as the United States has testified on more than one occasion. We insist on bonds of the kind I described some time ago, where boats laden with liquor come from across the ocean, or from St. Pierre Miquelon, which is the centre of the trade, and enter Halifax harbour; at least they used to enter that harbour in stress or storm or from any other cause. They now must give .a bond in the same way as die others that export to foreign countries. The result is that that business has stopped altogether, and the depots that were formed1 in Nova Scotia, from which liquor was smuggled into the United States, are no longer in existence. In addition to that we closed the export houses to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred. There were in Canada so-called export houses-houses which imported liquor, stored it in these places in bond, and then exported it. I think i't is true to say that perhaps 95 per cent of the liquor in these export bond houses went to the United States. We have closed these and shut out that source of supply to the United States, because this department agreed with the royal commission that these customs bonds served no useful purpose; and although it is quite true that the Dominion government obtained considerable revenue from that source, it was not taken into consideration at all. We passed last session the Intoxicating Liquors Act; the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) piloted that bill through the house. The result is that now, with a few exceptions, no other than the local control authorities in any province may import liquor into that provinoe. That also has prevented the accumulation of liquor which later found its way into the United States. We have limited in Ontario, where most of the export business is done, the number of docks from which liquor may be exported.

The house resumed from May 7, consideration in committee of Bill No. 75, respecting the domicile of married women in proceedings for divorce-Mr. Ward-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 2-Married woman separate from husband.

maintopic: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
When this bill was
before the house the other evening objections were voiced to it as it stands, and at that time a proposed motion was placed before the house but was not put as there was no seconder. The proposal contained in that amendment was also objected to when it came before the house. The discussion brought out very clearly that there is a real need in Canada for some such legislation as is proposed in this bill. The hon. leader of the opposition, when the bill was up before, explained some of the difficulties that the courts in Canada have to face in- connection with our divorce legislation, and the references that he made to various cases which have been decided showed clearly that there is a real need for some such legislation as is here proposed. In order to meet some of the difficulties that were mentioned in the discussion, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk, that sections 2 and 3 of the bill be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
2. A married woman who either before or after the passing of this act has been deserted by and has lived separate and apart from her husband for a period of two years and upwards and is still living separate and apart from her husband may acquire in any one of the provinces of Canada in which there is a court having jurisdiction to grant a divorce a vinculo matrimonii a domicile of her own choice as though she were a feme sole for the purpose of commencing in the province in which she has acquired such domicile an action for divorce a vinculo matrimonii praying that her marriage may be dissolved on any grounds that may entitle her to such divorce in the court of such province having jurisdiction to grant such divorce whatever the domicile of the husband may be, provided that for the purpose aforesaid such married woman shall be deemed to retain the domicile of her husband at the time she was so deserted until she has acquired a domicile of her own choice as aforesaid.
The amendment meets the objection that was raised the other evening that the bill as it stands goes too far and might encroach
Divorce Proceedings-Domicile

upon other situations than that of divorce, because it clearly and definitely limits the domicile to the purpose of divorce. As the bill is changed by this amendment I can see no objection to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I objected to the bill on the two occasions when it came before the committee, first, as originally drafted, and afterwards as amended. I must admit that as far as the constitutional side is concerned, the new amendment is not subject to criticism as were the two first drafts. But speaking for myself I am sorry to say that I still object to the bill, and I would regret if it should become the law of this country. I wish to repeat what I have stated as to the various effects of this bill if it passes parliament. For instance, a wife will foe able to take proceedings for divorce in Manitoba or in Saskatchewan, while her husband1 may apply to this parliament for divorce if he still lives either in Ontario or in Quebec. There may be two applications for divorce in two different places. There may be even two divorce trials before two different courts if the wife goes to another province where there is a divorce court. There may foe two actions for divorce, and there will be a race for the better position. I still believe in the soundness of the British doctrine in this respect, that there is only one, and that there should be and can be but one, domicile as long as the matrimonial tie continues, and that only when it is dissolved can there be two domiciles.
My regret more particularly is that this bill if enacted would provide greater facilities for divorce. Public men in other countries have regretted the increased facilities for divorce, but once the door has been opened it is very difficult to close it. We in this country have always boasted that our record is clean in this respect. I admit that I do not share the viewpoint of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, that it is better that we should have the facilities which this bill will provide to avoid the scandal of some of our people going to the country to the south of us and there building up a fictitious domicile to obtain a divorce which has more or less legal effect in Canada. I repeat I do not agree with my hon. friend in that regard. I think it is better for us to keep our record clean in this respect, and that the remedy will be worse than the disease.
Our conditions are very similar in so many respects with those that prevail in the United States that I am afraid the troubles that are regretted over there will become ours if we adopt their system and make our laws concerning marriage and divorce more like those of that country than those of Great Britain.

The strength of our Canadian life has been based to a large extent on our marriage laws, and I do not think there is anywhere in Canada much public opinion in favour of changing those laws. Among all classes of our ipeople marriage is respected. Our people everywhere have always believed that once a man and a woman are united in marriage, the union is for better or for worse, and1 that it is a lifelong contract. This has always been the Canadian conviction, and we have been proud of it. I still think that by the adoption of this measure we should be entering on a new policy fraught with danger to our national life, and for that reason I cannot agree with the amendment and shall register my vote against it.

maintopic: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I regret
my inability to agree with the Minister of Justice in respect to this matter. I think he has overlooked one or two essential factors that should be considered. First of all, this bill does not extend the causes for which divorce may be obtained. The only ground upon which divorce may be obtained is unfaithfulness. Secondly, it must be remembered that the wife in order to obtain a separate domicile must be deserted by the husband. If she has lived in the domicile where the husband has deserted her, by this bill she merely will be able to maintain her action there on the assumption that he having gone away, she knows not where, has for the purposes of the action left her with the domicile where she was deserted. There can be no scandal in that. If by reason of her desertion she finds it necessary to leave the community where she lives and go to some other province, she can acquire domicile only by satisfying the court of two facts, because domicile is a question of fact: (a) residence and (b) intention to remain in that jurisdiction. When these two factors are present and the court finds as a matter of fact that the wife is thus domiciled, this legislation will confer upon that court the necessary jurisdiction to enable that action to be maintained. How can it be successfully said in this age, when a woman may hold property and, under the Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857, shall, if judicially separated from her husband, be regarded as a feme sole and, as such, may for every purpose in the world be deemed an unmarried woman, that she shall nevertheless, for the purpose of separating herself from her spouse, who has been unfaithful, be unable to acquire that necessary ingredient to enable the court to exercise its jurisdiction, namely, domicile? How can we take the view in this day and generation that she shall not be considered to have a separate domicile in a matter

Export of Liquor-Mr. Euler
of this kind, because by a fiction of law "they two are one"? It must not be forgotten that the principle of British law, to which my hon. friend has referred, is a principle based upon that old saying-"They two shall be one, and the husband is that one." In France, in Germany and in other continental countries where the question has been considered it has been conceded that the adandoned wife may acquire a domicile inasmuch as she is in the eyes of the law a separate entity, her existence being no longer merged in that of her husband. And since there is no longer any merging of her identity or personality in that of her husband, and she may exercise the power of a feme sole, as we have evidence of in legislatures and parliament and other institutions of the country, I do not think we are going to the extent indicated by the minister when we merely confer upon the appropriate court the power to exercise its jurisdiction upon its being satisfied that a woman who has been deserted and abandoned by her husband1-he having been guilty of unfaithfulness-has acquired, by virtue of residence and intention, that domicile which will enable her to prosecute and maintain her action for the termination of the marriage tie by reason of such infidelity.

maintopic: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
Before the bill is carried
I want to state my views on this matter. I wish to say first of all that what astounds me is that every particular case will be decided under this act. Now every case is entirely different from every other. In the province of Quebec, when a wife asks for separation from bed and board, she presents a petition to the judge seeking the right to have a separate domicile temporarily until judgment is given. The judge listens to the arguments in support of the petition, and if he deems it advisable to grant the wife a domicile separate from that of her husband he granted the petition. On the other hand, if, according to the evidence, it does not seem to him proper to grant the petition, he refuses it. The matter is left to the good judgment and experience of the judge. But more than that, judges of the superior court of the province of Quebec very often 'in these cases try to bring the two parties together; in his chambers the judge places the situation before them and hears what they have to say. Sometimes the separation is asked for merely because the parties for some reason or other cannot agree, but the cause of difference is not so serious as they imagine and the judge tries to conciliate them. Consequently the suit is very often abandoned by reason of the very sensible course followed by the judge, who exercises
his office for the benefit of both parties concerned.
Some arguments brought forward in this discussion are rather strange. Someone has said that in such a case the wife should have the same rights as the husband. Well, undoubtedly the wife has as many rights as the husband, but they are not of the same kind; it makes all the difference in the world. For guidance, are we going to go back four centuries ago when the Indians had camps here, and on this very spot where now stands this beautiful parliament of Canada? At that time the squaws had many powers and rights; they used to go out hunting while the husband kept the home fires burning.

maintopic: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS
subtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to inform the house whether he is Speaking for the bill or against it? It is nearly nine o'clock and we should like to know.

maintopic: DIVORCE PROCEEDINGS

speechtext:
Well, you may call this
an exordium; I am giving you the general lines of my speech. Afterwards I shall come to what we call the confirmation of the speech, and I shall then submit stronger arguments to support my view. Someone has said in this debate that the wife should have the same rights as the husband. That may be all right; but that matter is not in question at all. I cannot agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when ho dismisses as fictitious the idea of unity as between man and wife. It is not merely saying that husband and wife shall be one; it is more than that It is a question of the very existence of the family.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance) for the house to go into committee of supply.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
When the house rose at
six o'clock I was discussing the measures which had already been taken by the Department of National Revenue to limit the carrying of liquor to the United States. I
Export of Liquor-Mr. Euler

stated that we had agreed to the right of search within the twelve-mile limit by United States vessels of ships supposed to be carrying liquor to that country. I stated also that we had agreed under the treaty to give information to the United States of all clearances of vessels leaving Canadian ports and carrying liquor to the United States. As I said this afternoon, that agreement has been faithfully carried out, and statements to that effect have been made by the United States government.
I might have made reference to a rather remarkable condition existing at Windsor in connection with the giving of notices to United States customs authorities. As I said this afternoon, Windsor is one of the chief ports of liquor export to the United States. Under the treaty the collector at the port of Windsor did give notice by telephone to the United States customs authorities at Detroit of clearances that had been given. I am not going to suggest any reason, but peculiarly enough we were requested by the United States government to discontinue the giving of telephone notices to the collector at Detroit, and in accordance with that request such notices were no longer given at that port. They asked us then to give weekly reports rather than daily reports by telephone, and we have acceded to their request.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Was that the United States federal government?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes. I further said that
we are now demanding bonds for all liquorladen vessels coming from abroad and entering Canadian ports, no matter what the reason may be. In the past that was made an excuse for landing some of these liquors in Canada, thus providing a convenient means of later transporting it to the United States. The result of our action in demanding these bonds has been to stop that method entirely.
In addition, we have taken steps to close all the export bond liquor houses in Canada; while I mentioned that fact this afternoon I forgot to mention one other point. These houses imported liquor from abroad and stored it in bond for the purpose of later exporting it to the United States. We decided that these houses should be closed, that they served no useful purpose but promoted the exportation of liquor to the United States, We took action to close them, but under the law any liquor in bond could remain there for two years. No further liquor has been allowed to come into these houses for many months, and the liquor remaining there must
[Mr. Euler.3
be exported in about a year from now, I believe some time in June, 1930. Then this system, which was a very fertile source of exportation of liquor to the United States, will be done away with entirely.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
How many of these
houses remain in that position?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I think there are one or two in British Columbia and one in Halifax, but in June of 1930 these places will be out of business and in the meantime they cannot import further stocks. I said this afternoon that we also passed the Intoxicating Liquors Act, which gave to the provincial authorities the sole right to import liquor. That again circumscribes the power of export to the United States.
At six o'clock I was referring to the fact that in certain parts of Ontario we had limited the number of docks from which liquor could be exported, and perhaps it would be interesting to the house if I reviewed what led up to that action. At the interprovincial conference held in the fall of 1927 I agreed to cooperate in every reasonable way with the provincial authorities in the enforcement of the provincial liquor laws. One of the results of that agreement was the passage of the Intoxicating Liquors Act, although that act had been introduced the year previously. We further agreed that no additional licenses for distilleries or breweries should be issued anywhere in Canada by the Department of National Revenue without first consulting with the provincial authorities, and I may say that unless some arrangement had been made prior to the agreement with the provinces, in no case has a license been issued except with the consent of such provincial authority.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Does that "consultation"
necessarily mean "consent"?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
We are not bound by it,
but I may say that the minister has so far followed the wishes of the provinces. I do not think, however, he should bind himself entirely; circumstances might arise which would lead him to believe that such licenses should be granted, but the fact is that no such license has been issued since that arrangement with the provincial authorities was arrived at, and I propose to continue that policy.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: What date was that?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The promise of cooperation was made at the interprovincial conference, and the actual agreement with the provinces was arrived at some months later. I think it has been in existence about a year, or perhaps a little longer.

Export of Liquor-Mr. Euler
Something was said this afternoon with regard to short-circuiting; it was suggested that the export of liquor to the United States made it possible to short-circuit liquor into the different provinces without any great trouble. I believe that statement has been made by the chairman of the Ontario Liquor Control Board, Sir Henry Drayton. I am not altogether prepared to contradict him, but I do not think there is very much short-circuiting of liquor in the province of Ontario, because any man who desires liquor can purchase it without trouble at the stores of the Liquor Control Board. There may be a little short-circuiting which comes about in this way:	Occasionally a boat which sails from
the Ontario side, perhaps from the port of Windsor, finds it impossible to land the cargo on the other side and is forced to turn back and land that cargo of liquor somewhere in Ontario.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
That seems to be a rare
occurrence.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I think it is quite rare. We
have further instituted a system of checking all shipments of liquor from the docks into the boats; our officers carry on that work. We are also abolishing what was termed the nuisance and abuse of the B-13 forms connected with the shipment of beer; we are now inaugurating a new system of permits which I think will remove most of the complaints of the provincial authorities. As a matter of fact, as I said this afternoon, the number of docks at the border in the Windsor district has been reduced from fifty to ten. That was done absolutely with the cooperation of the provincial authorities; the selection of these docks was made by the collector at Windsor in conjunction with the inspector working under Sir Henry Drayton. Perhaps I should not take any undue credit for trying to assist the United States in regard to the limitation of docks; I will admit that it was done for the sole purpose of assisting in the enforcement of the Ontario Liquor Control Act. It was felt that if the number of docks were limited the Ontario authorities could more closely watch the operations of the exporters and take precautions in order to see that there would be no Short-circuiting. However, the result has been that the United States authorities have been given, if they choose to avail themselves of it, a similar opportunity to watch the operation of these exporters and protect their own shores.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I understand that we receive no landing certificates for these cargoes of
liquor, but what certificate is received from the American authorities showing that the vessel which cleared from Windsor has arrived at Detroit?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
We receive none; we are
not entitled to any under the law. We cannot even demand a certificate showing that a landing has been made in another country, when the boat returns to Canadian shores. That question has been brought up before; we have consulted with the Department of Justice and that is the law.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Is it not true that a
number of those docks which were closed were merely little unimportant docks or jetties?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, that is quite true; some of them were very unimposing places, but still they were shipping liquor. It had been thought, and corresponding criticism had been made in the press until about a year ago, that the Minister of National Revenue had authority to discontinue the issuance of clearances to boats exporting liquor to the United States. Probably my hon. friend, (Mr. Stevens) who was minister for a short time before I took over the department, had the same thought; I may be wrong but I think he found, as I did upon making inquiry, that there %vas no power under the act for the minister to refuse clearances in that way. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I think that the department and the government have done practically everything which could be done under the law as it now stands to help our neighbours, short of the actual prohibition of exports. It should be remembered that after all Canada is not a prohibitionist country. That fact may be regretted by a great many estimable people, and many of them may be in this house. I have no fault to find with that, but the fact remains that under our law liquor may be manufactured and sold in Canada under certain conditions. We have a system of public control for the making and the sale of liquors and we have been quite consistent in the matter of limiting the number of docks, which implies control but does not imply prohibition.
It is quite apparent that in order to bring about the result which is desired by the United States, and by our friends who have spoken prior to myself, it is necessary that the law be changed before the issuance of clearances can be stopped.
I would like to sum up very briefly what seem to me to be the reasons both for and against a policy of that kind. It has been said that we are violating the spirit of the treaty



Export of Liquor

Mr. Euler
tvhich was made in 1924 by not absolutely prohibiting the exportation of liquors. I cannot agree with that and I do not think it is a fair charge. As I stated this afternoon, before the treaty was actually made the United States asked that the export of liquor should be made illegal, that no clearances should be granted; that is what it wanted but the Canadian government did not grant that. It seems to me that if it was the intention of the Canadian government to stop the export of liquors it would have been specifically stated in the treaty which was made; that seems to me to be absolutely logical, and it is just as reasonable to suppose that what was specifically stated in the treaty was as far as we cared to go at that time. I refer to the obligation which we are carrying out, to give notice of clearance whenever a boat leaves the Canadian shore.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Go on, go on.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: He is a minister replying.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: With the unanimous consent of the house.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I thank the members for their very courteous indulgence and I promise not to impose unduly upon their patience.
This question has been discussed very freely and I tlhinlc it is only fair to give at this time some of the facts which I think have not been brought out. One argument which impresses me most strongly in favour of the prohibition of exports is the moral argument. It has been stated that the business of the exportation of liquor has resulted in the demoralization of people and has increased the disregard for law generally. I believe that, to some extent, that is the fact, a fact very much to be deplored, and one which I do not think any member of this house will condone. It will be agreed that wherever a country is under a prohibitory law to which a very large minority is opposed, the condition which has been described is inescapable.
It has been stated that other countries prohibit the issuance of clearances, and Great Britain was cited by the United States authorities in that connection. As a matter of fact we have made, inquiry, and there is no such practice in Great Britain. That country does not refuse clearances for the exportation of liquor to atiy other country in the world, so far as I know.
Petitions by the hundreds have been presented to this house asking that clearances be
(Mr. Euler.]
no longer issued. I believe that the petitioners have so petitioned because they are opposed absolutely to the traffic in liquor. I do not believe that they were moved primarily by their regard for the feelings of a friendly nation; I believe that the prime motive was as I have stated, but I must say that I have no fault to find with that motive. I might say in passing-perhaps I should not sa]' this, but I will-that to me it does not seem quite consistent that we as a country, or as separate provinces, should permit the legal manufacture and sale of liquor and then place undue restrictions upon the sale of liquor anywhere else.
One of the arguments offered against our prohibiting the issuance of clearances is that the problem which the United States is now experiencing is one of their own making and that we are not primarily responsible. Another is-using the words of the man on the street-"Let the United States enforce their own law." In the light of the statements which I made this afternoon, in connection with the lack of effort on the part of the United States to enforce their own law, I think that attitude is a very human and fairly reasonable one and that we might at least go slowly until we have some assurance and some evidence that they are trying to do for themselves what they are now asking us to do for them.
I mentioned this afternoon the peculiar fact that whereas we in Canada compel all boats, no matter how small, to take clearances when they leave our shores and to report when they return, that practice does not obtain in the United States. All boats under five tons sailing from United States ports are not required to take clearances and do not report when they return, yet practically all the boats engaged in this traffic are of United States registry and the great majority of them are of a tonnage less than five. Perhaps I should not offer advice to the United States as to what they should do, but it seems to me it would not be unreasonable for us to say, when they ask us not to give clearances to small boats, that they should amend their own law and demand clearances from their boats when they leave a port and ask them to report when they return, thus obtaining control over their own boats.
The statement has been made frequently that it is Canadian liquor which is flooding the United States. There is no reasonable doubt that a large amount of liquor does go from Canada into the United States, but relatively speaking the amount is very small
Export of Liquor-Mr. Euler

based upon the evidence of United States authorities connected with the enforcement of their law that it is only from two to five per cent of their total consumption which is imported from Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to offer the most important argument as I see it. Suppose for the moment that it is thought desirable to accede to the request of the United States and to the requests of the many petitioners who have come to this parliament, and that we pas a law prohibiting the issuance of clearances. In my opinion, if that remedy were adopted it would not solve the difficult}'. Liquor can be obtained throughout Canada quite freely. In the province of Ontario liquor may be purchased in fairly large quantities from the government stores. In the province of Quebec they have the right under their law, although it is not exercised, to sell any quantity for export by the Quebec Liquor Commission. Liquor may be bought in fairly large quantities in almost every province of the Dominion. If clearances were not issued perhaps the quantity exported would not be so large, but there is no doubt in my mind that a great deal of liquor would be purchased throughout the Dominion of Canada for the purpose of exportation to the United States. If clearances would no longer be granted; the result would be that shipments of liquor to the United States w'ould not go from recognized customs ports on the Canadian border, and the traffic would be forced underground to the corruption of Canadian people where perhaps it has not extended to Canada as it has to the United States. That would be a very undesirable situation. Moveover, probably the liquor that now goes across the border might successfully be shipped down to ocean ports and perhaps exported to St. Pierre and Miquelon, which also takes no particular precautions as to where the liquor is going, and from whose exports we in Canada suffer very considerably. One of the worst troubles we have m connection with preventive measures in the maritimes is that the St. Pierre and Miquelon islands lie at our doors and it is impossible to prevent the smuggling of liquor from those islands into our own country. It seems to me that in that case, if the liquor cannot go out through a recognized customs port in Canada, it will go out through perhaps every little landing place that may exist along our boundaries lined with lakes and rivers.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: And worse liquor.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Perhaps worse liquor, and
the difficulty from our point of view will be that it will then be illegally exported. As 78594-172J
the matter stands now, the export of liquor from Canada is absolutely legal. The illegality arises where the liquor enters the United States, because the importation of liquor into that country is against their law. Exportation of liquor from Canada is entirely legal. If we pass a law prohibiting clearance, the liquor will then go out in any case, but it will go out illegally and secretly instead of openly, aboveboard and subject to a certain amount of observation, because we have limited the-number of places from which exportation cart be made.
I mentioned this afternoon that when the-excise was paid on liquor manufactured in Canada, the liquor became free goods and could be exported the same as any other commodity. I repeat that because I want to add this further observation: that being the case, we cannot stop the exportation of that liquor from any customs port in the Dominion. We have limited the number of docks, but that has not resulted in stopping the exportation of liquor through those ports. We can limit the number of docks within any one port, as we did, for example, at Windsor; but we cannot, under the present law, stop the export through any open port in the Dominion. There are those who say-and I have in mind now particularly a prominent Toronto newspaper-that if we passed a law prohibiting the granting of clearances, we would at least have washed our national hands of an offence against a friendly neighbour, and that, having done that, we would be under no Obligation to spend money or time to uphold the laws of the United States. I cannot agree with that view. I cannot escape the conclusion that we then assume a responsibility which now rests upon the United States. As the matter stands, if there is any violation of law it is a violation of United States law. As it would be under the new law, it would be a violation of Canadian customs law. The iaw is the law, and we cannot shirk responsibility as readily as that suggestion would meke it appear. If a Canadian customs law is violated, surely it becomes the duty of Canadian customs officers to see that that violation is punished. I am not trying to exaggerate; I do not think I am drawing a fanciful picture at all, but I say that if we are under an obligation in the Department of National Revenue to see that violations of the law are punished, surely we shall need to establish a preventive force a good deal larger than the one we have now, which, I may say, is giving me enough trouble as it is. I am sure the most ardent prohibitionist wilt not say that this country should be under

Export of Liquor-Mr. Euler
any obligation to spend large sums of money in employing many men to see that that law prohibiting the exportation of liquor is not violated. Nations have not yet become quite so altruistic as that. Besides that, we would not succeed; we could not stop the exportation of liquor, although it might be lessened to some extent. After we had passed a law of that kind and liquor still continued to flow into the United States, I feel sure that our neighbours would yet be much inclined to criticize and we would continue to get the blame.
So far as I am concerned-and I think I can speak for the government in this matter -we are honestly anxious to do all that we reasonably can to assist our neighbours. But I will also say very frankly that I am more concerned with stopping smuggling into Canada than stopping smuggling into the United States. The first is our own particular business and the other is primarily theirs. The Department of National Revenue, as it is now with its many branches and ramifications, provides plenty of work for those connected with that department. It is a fairly big job and I will admit I have no inclination at the present moment to add more duties to that department which has already so many. I am not deliberately looking for more trouble. I admit the problem is a difficult one and it gives the government some concern.
Personally-and I think I may again speak for the government in this-I have received with considerable sympathy and every consideration the protests of those who are opposed to the exportation of liquor, but I sincerely believe that under all the circumstances as related by myself this afternoon and evening, and with all the measures already taken, the government has done fairly well, and has perhaps gone far enough. But the door is not closed; the government is always prepared to give further consideration is developments may justify it. I feel, how-sver, that- before we take any further action there should be more convincing proof that our neighbours are sincerely doing all they can to help themselves. In the meantime the government desires and welcomes a frank discussion by members of all parties of a difficult and vexing problem, in order to enable it to arrive at new conclusions or to be 'confirmed in the position that so far has been taken.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house as a whole will agree with me when I say that the minister has given a very frank and
(Mr. Euler.]
carefully studied statement of a most difficult problem. Personally I congratulate him upon the clarity of his utterances; and with the greater part of what he has said little fault can be found. I should like briefly to bring to the attention of the house one or two points arising out of what he has said.
There are perhaps two main suggestions arising out of his remarks: first, it must be granted by every hon. member that the problem is an exceedingly complicated and difficult one. Second, by the official statements of the Minister of National Revenue in charge of the administration of the customs and excise of the Dominion of Canada made in the house to-day regarding the manner in which the officers administering the law on the other side Of the line have reciprocated, shall I say, the courtesies and the efforts that the minister declares his officers have made, there is presented to the house an appalling situation. The minister told us most frankly, and in clear and unmistakable language, that under a solemn treaty entered into between the two countries Canada had agreed to render to a friendly neighbouring state the service of notifying them when vessels laden with liquor cleared from Canada for points in the United States; that these vessels have been cleared from Canada in a perfectly legal manner for the last few years; that Canadian officers had promptly, and in some cases twice for the same vessel, notified the official at the United States point to which the vessel was going of the name of the vessel, the name of the officer in charge, and the nature of the cargo; that these vessels left Canadian ports, Bridgeburg, Windsor and other points in broad daylight; that they proceeded across the river, and that the actual unloading of the cases of liquor themselves could be seen from the Canadian side, and yet in the work of unloading they were unmolested and not interfered with by the American officers, although in every case the American officers had been advised of the departure or prospective departure of the vessels, in some cases only two hours prior to sailing. Further, it has been declared that with very few exceptions these boats are American-owned boats, the names of which are well known to the officials on the American side, and that finally, little or no notice is taken of this courtesy on the part of Canada in the discharge of her duties under the treaty. The minister further tells us that [DOT] the American government had requested that the notification in regard to the Windsor-Detroit traffic should be discontinued.

Export oj Liquor-Mr. Stevens

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
They requested that the
notification sent daily by telephone should be sent weekly, and not by telephone.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Yes, that the practice
of modifying them by telephone, as was the understanding, should foe 'discontinued and that notification should be sent weekly instead of every day. These statements, coming as they do from a minister of the crown in the House of Commons, and from a minister of the crown noted for the coolness and dieliiberatemess of his utterances, present to this parliament a situation which I think warrants our attention. I miake this suggestion to the Prime Minister-I have not had time to consult either with my leader or with those around me, and. I am therefore discussing this matter on my own responsibility, simply as a member of the house-I suggest, to the Prime Minister that a treaty such as that which we have made genuine efforts to observe, the United States authorities apparently taking no notice of these efforts on our part, might very well be dispensed with and abrogated. It seems to me that the treaty is a farce. I must say that the picture drawn by the minister presents a situation which if I can judge of the temper of the people south of the line will cause them a good deal of anxiety and will perturb the mind at least of the government there for some time to come.
There are two o,r three things that I should like very greatly to discuss. On one of them the minister touched lightly, but I think he will not disagree with me when I say that it is clear that the practice of certain persons, largely American citizens, from what the minister tells us, in continually violating the American laws is building up a spirit of lawlessness which is reflected not only in the smuggling of liquor but in much more violent ways. I think it is known the world over, it is certainly known all over this continent, that in Detroit and Chicago and other American cities the violent crimes directly attributable to this traffic are nothing short of appalling. I recall reading only a few weeks ago an address by the president of the United States to the press association of the United States, pointing to the number of murders 'Committed in one of the great American cities, the number of convictions, and the number of apprehensions due largely, but not wholly, of course, to this traffic. I have not the statement with me, but it seemed to me unbelievable. That feature, I think, warrants the attention of the government of this country as well as
that of the United States. We cannot lightly brush it aside on the ground that some of us may be in favour of a prohibitory measure and some of us opposed to it. That is not the ground from which that class of criminality can be viewed, and anything that contributes to such a situation merits the closest scrutiny of parliament itself.
What is lying at the bottom of all this? At the bottom of it all is the profit that is in it. There is one aspect of the matter which I should like to present to the house and to the government. Last year, according to returns which I have received, the Dominion of Canada collected from the distillers in this country, by way of excise duty the sum of $12,400,000. Of that amount, $7,800,000 was duty paid on spirits exported to the United States, and $4,600,000 on domestic spirits, or spirits consumed in Canada. I pause to impress upon the attention of the house the significance of those figures. Under the Excise Act as I read it there are only two ways in which the release of spirits may be treated; one is for domestic consumption, where an excise duty of $9 a gallon is imposed, and the other is for export, where this $9 excise duty is refunded. But in recent years, owing to the development of this illicit traffic to the United States-illicit only so far as entry to the United States is concerned-we have introduced a third class of duty, namely, the collection of the regidar home consumption excise duty of $9 a gallon on such liquor as is exported to the United States. I submit that in my opinion that excise duty ought not to be collected. I put it upon this basis: After all, the minister was perfectly correct in his statement that this is a legal business in Canada. I made the statement three years ago, and again last year, that just so long as the manufacture and safe of liquor is legalized in Canada, just so long are those in the business entitled to fair and equitable treatment by the administrative authorities of this country, dominion and provincial. I conceive that neither this nor any other government has the right to single out this particular business and say: We will impose a tax upon you in respect of all the liquor exported to the United States, but we shall not impose it upon liquor exported to Cuba, Porto Rico, China, Japan, England, and so forth. A very considerable quantity of liquor is exported to other countries. I have not the figures before me, but speaking from memory, .last year the total export was some 1,800,000 gallons, whereas the export to the United States was 1,100,000 gallons-in round figures showing about one third was exported to other countries.
270S

Export of Liquor-Mr. Stevens
That trade paid no excise tax-it was fully refunded; but the 1,000,000 gallons going to the United States were taxed. To the extent that we collect that revenue and allow the fact of the $7,000,000 from that source to influence the mind of parliament, we are partners in this export business to the United States. I think we might as well frankly face that situation. I know there is a schodl of thought in Canada which argues that if we can make a dollar out of the export of liquor to the United ' States-well, let the Yankee pay it. I remember that one of the witnesses who appeared before the customs committee, a man by the name of Cooper, made an immense fortune out of this business. By the way, it was recommended that he should be sued for some $900,000, but I do not know whether the case was proceeded with or not. He made the statement that it was a splendid thing for Canada to get "the good American dollar," as he put it. I submit it is not in the interests of Canada's self respect that for the sake of a revenue of $7,000,000 we should actually become partners in the business of export of liquor to the United States.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I do not like to interrupt,
Ibut may I ask a question?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My forty minutes are
just as short as the minister's.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I merely wish to ask this
question. The hon. member suggests that we should not collect excise tax on liquors exported to the United States. Does he mean that the liquor should be allowed to be exported without paying the tax?

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I did not put it quite that way.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: I submit that this is not a laughing matter.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: My question is quite serious.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I will try to express myself clearly to the minister. I do not think this is a matter that should be treated lightly. I want to say to the Prime Minister and his government that I am not approaching the question in any captious spirit, nor do I intend to do so during these remarks. I repeat, under the statutes as I read them, the practice-leaving out of the question for the moment the export to the United States -in years gone by was to treat the taxing of liquor on two bases, one, that Canadian-made liquor exported was not taxed, that is, the excise tax was not imposed; two, that on

liquor manufactured in Canada for consumption in Canada an excise tax was imposed of $9 a gallon. But there has now grown up a third basis, namely the imposition of an excise duty of $9 a gallon on liquor exported to the United States. To put it a little differently, the exact form of that tax is this: the excise duty of $9 a gallon is paid on all this liquor, and it is refunded where the liquor is exported to foreign countries, except to the United States. I submit that that in a sense makes us a partner in this business of trafficking in intoxicating liquor to the United States-indirectly, not directly. I submit further that that is not conducive to the dignity of this country.
When I was interrupted I was proceeding to say that at the bottom of this business is the money that is in it. Let me give to the house the profit which accrues to those engaged in it. The minister will correct me if I am wrong in my figures; I think I am not. Whiskey constitutes the great bulk of the liquor traffic. Each case of whiskey contains 12 bottles or 2 gallons. The excise tax is $9 a gallon or $18 a case. That is, the Dominion of Canada takes $18 a case in the form of excise tax. If the goods are sold in Canada by some province there is a wide margin of profit. I will give the figures for my own province as they used to be; I think they still apply. They have a profit of $20 a case. That makes the cost $38 a case. According to the returns of the Department of Trade and Commerce, whiskey costs to produce $2.65 a gallon, or about $5.50 a case. On an article worth about $5 or $6 the Dominion tax and the profit of the province represent about $38. In the case of imported liquor it is $40. If the bootlegger or smuggler bringing in liquor from outside can sell without the province knowing it he has a margin of $20 a case upon which to work; if he can evade the excise duties or customs duties, he has another $20, that is, a margin of $40 a case. The point I make is that the monetary inducement to violate the law is simply terrific. Last year I suggested, and I suggest again now, that it would be good business on the part of the parliament of Canada if we made a very drastic revision in the import duties and the excise duties and so take away a substantial portion of this attractive profit offered to the illicit dealer in liquor. Secondly-and perhaps this is not my business, but I will mention it-if the provinces under the government sales system would merely add a profit that would take care of the cost of the distribution of the liquor

Export oj Liquor-Mr. Stevens
with a margin of safety, it would largely do away with the inducement to deal illicitly in liquor in this country.
Now I come to the suggestion of the minister that there would be no advantage in refusing clearances. In one sense I agree with the minister that perhaps there would be no advantage. But I should like to submit this to him. If we lowered our excise and also our customs duty we would of course lose a certain amount of revenue, but I am again pointing out that if you are going into this business for the revenue that is in it, then you must take the consequences of the persistent evasion of the law, whether in Canada or outside of Canada. But I assume that we are not in the business for the purpose of making money. It is a legal business and we want those in it to make reasonable profits and to act legally. Assuming that is the basis upon which we are to deal with it, then I say the minister can very well refuse clearances and not experience the result that he suggests, namely, that an underground system would be worked out. The only reason for an underground method being developed would be the excessive profits in the business. No men will go into this business and risk their lives, as they do daily and hourly-many of them, I think far more than we have any idea of, losing their lives-they will not go into the business except for the exorbitant profits in it. I am not going to take the minister to task on his suggestion that to refuse clearance would simply develop an. underground and illicit trade, but I do wish to suggest to him that at the present time we are actually facilitating the business. Let me put it to the minister this way. Had \ve not charged the distillers of Canada $9 a gallon and then given them in return for that $9 of revenue a free right of way to the export docks, and every possible official facility to get their liquor out of the country -had we not done that, or, to state the case differently, if we surrendered the $9 a gallon, we should not have to give that service. What we are actually doing is giving them that facility, that protection, and collecting $9 for it. In the first place I contend that the minister ought not to collect the $9 a gallon; they ought to be given the right to export, as they export to Cuba or China, or any other country. That is my first point. My second point is that it is not the business of the government to facilitate the moving of liquor to the boundary line for export. That is the business of the dealer in liquor.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: We don't do that.

The minister says he does not want to create a monopoly, but I would infinitely rather have seen the distilling business remain where it was ten years ago, in the hands of a few outstanding and reputable firms, than distributed over this long list of some twenty-five distilleries in Canada. Listening to the remarks which were made this afternoon one might think that all the crimes perpetuated in Chicago are due to the importation of Canadian liquor into the Lhaited States, but I think this is a great exaggeration. At the root of the liquor trade is not only the profit but also, the pleasure which some people derive from drinking liquor. This has been elementary since the days of Noah; it is quite an old principle, and it is well known that even in the United States liquor is sold on doctor's prescription. However, they take such great care to prevent the smuggling of liquor into that country that even diplomats must drive their own cars when they contain embassy liquor, and I do not mean Embassy Scotch. I have in my hand an article which appeared in the New York Times and which is as follows:
Diplomat Drives Car With Embassy Liquor.
By This Means Load Is Enabled To Pass Safely In Streets Of Washington.
Washington, March 13: The truck was accompanied by a member of the diplomatic corps, who personally took over the steering wheel and drove the truck into the city. In one case an attache of an embassy was following a truck in his private automobile, but this was not thought sufficient to give the truck immunity from seizure for carrying liquors. These warnings were given by the police before the passage of the Jones law, imposing more severe penalties for dry law violators.
This is very severe. I also remember having read in the papers that Lady Heath, I think, came from Great Britain with a bottle of champagne to christen a ship in the United States, and the bottle was seized. I have another clipping from the New York Times which contains the picture of an aviator and his wife, with these words underneath:

Captain William Lancaster, a British aviator.
holding the compass which was brought from England by Mrs. Lancaster and held up at the customs because it contained four ounces of pure alcohol. It was later passed.
Then I have an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 20:
Until Death Do Us Part
Ycars ago Macaulay spoke of the United States as being "all sail and no anchor." Reading the American press these days, with their tales of machine guns in the streets of Chicago, of 10,000 stills discovered in "dry" Pennsylvania, of thousands of undetected murderers, of bandits and crooked bosses, of bootleggers and hi-jackers, of domestic scandals and civic graft, one thinks of Macaulay's phrase.
Further in this article I find this paragraph:
Dudley G. Newcomb had a "love for liquor," said his wife. The judge thought he detected an odour at the hearing. Wherefore the court ruled $75 a month alimony to Mrs. Newcomb. Mr. Newcomib going to jail for contempt because of his aromatic breath.
This happened under American law; and I am not through with it yet. There is not only the comical side of it, which lies in the exaggeration of these people who think that when they have uttered the word "law" they have done everything; there is more. I have another clipping from the Ottawa Journal referring to a despatch under date of December 31. It is a very sad case and will show how stupidly the law is enforced in the United States:
A Legal Monstrosity
A court clothed with the power, and representing the authority and majesty, of a great state of the neighbouring republic closed its record for the year_ 1928 with an act which for its revelation o'f the state of mind and folly that bigotry upon a public question can produce, should not go unheeded. "Lansing, Michigan, December 31: Mrs. Etta Miller, mother of ten children and grandmother of two, and the first woman convicted as a fourth offender under the new criminal code, was sentenced to life imprisonment in the Detroit House of Correction this afternoon, immediately after a jury, which had deliberated twenty minutes, returned a verdict of guilty. Her fourth offence was the sale of two pints of liquor."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one would think from the discussion that has taken place thus far that the request that clearances should not be granted to liquor cargoes going to the United States was made in the first instance by the delegation which visited Ottawa in January of this year. It is well, perhaps, that the United States delegation brought to our attention some of the recommendations that were made in the session of 1926 when the customs scandals were under investigation. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) this evening reminded us that the Ontario Liquor Control Board had requested one or two years ago that restrictions be tightened up at Windsor. The fact was that conditions became so intolerable in that district that the Border Cities Star, a very influential paper of Windsor, through a series of editorials complained of the conditions existing there. The Ontario government was forced to take action and it reminded the federal government of the recommendation of the royal commission and also of the committee that sat in this house in 1926 in connection with the smuggling situation. The recommendation was that the number of export docks should be reduced, and it was favourably considered by the Ontario Liquor Control Board and by the federal government. We are informed to-night that the number was reduced from about fifty to ten.
I wish to approach this question not from the viewpoint of the request of the United States delegation but entirely from our own viewpoint and our own concern. In the
session of 1926, when it was suggested that clearances should not be granted to cargoes of liquor bound for the United States, there was no thought that we were assisting the United States in enforcing their laws. The idea was that it was for our own good, for the benefit of this country and for that alone, that such a reform should be undertaken. It seems to me rather a superficial view to take of the situation to say that we should go rather slowly in assisting another nation to enforce their prohibtion laws when it is remembered that this question was under consideration for nearly a whole session in this parliament. A committee of this house brought in a report recommending that clearances be refused, and that report was adopted by the parliament of the day with all parties assenting thereto and not a dissenting voice in the whole house. The Prime Minister and the government of the day agreed that such should be dlone. The opposition, under a different leader from the hon. member occupying that position to-day, agreed that clearances should not be granted. The Progressive group in this part of the house were very anxious and insistent that all reforms along this line should be undertaken. As I say, the report of the committee was approved unanimously. Shortly after that the-whole question was thrown into the arena of a Dominion election. Definite assurances were given that the necessary measures would be taken to clear up the situation. The Prime Minister gave a pledge to that effect and' a royal commission was appointed which spent many months in investigating the whole liquor business and smuggling in general, although I may say that most of the smuggling was found to be in connection with liquor. The report of the commission revealed an appalling situation. 1'he liquor trade seemed to recognize no law whatsoever: they would not, in many instances, pay excise tax or make income tax or sales tax returns. I believe that .more than $4,000,000 have since been collected in back taxes from liquor firms.
The report of that royal commission was tabled only a short time ago, after a general election, before a new parliament, before a house whose personnel had largely changed, with many new members, and with a new leader of the opposition. That report recommended that the export of liquor be prohibited; that clearances be not granted. That report again was endorsed by every member of the house, by the government, by the opposition and by the party in this corner. There was not a dissenting voice. Why then should we hie away to the United States for an excuse to evade what at that time we
