Export oj Liquor-Mr. Fansher (Lambton)
deemed to be our responsibility in connection with this matter? I want to say at this juncture that a large section of the people of this Dominion has not lost sight of the promises made at that time, of the reports given to the house, and of the way in which they were received. Many of those people are very sincere when they petition the house at this session to have that recommendation enacted into law. The house has received petitions not only from temperance organizations but from women's institutes, township councils and various other organizations of a secular nature urging that the government carry out what both the committee and the royal commission recommended and what two parliaments adopted and agreed should be done. It is difficult for me to understand why this question should not now be considered from that viewpoint rather than from the viewpoint of assisting the United States in the enforcement of their law. The justice of the end sought I think demands that we should enact legislation which would refuse clearance to liquor cargoes going to the United States. Surely we are not interested in the trade to the extent that we are going to assist it by giving clearance to vessels landing contraband stuff in the country adjoining, but we should be interested, and I think we are interested as Canadian citizens in maintaining law and order in this country, and in maintaining the virility of our citizens.
I was astounded when I heard the Minister of National Revenue say that he was more interested in stopping smuggling into Canada than in prohibiting smuggling from Canada into the United States. I wondered by what process of reasoning he could figure out that he could curtail smuggling into this country when he says to the liquor exporters, citizens of this country perhaps only temporarily, but many of them citizens of this country for a good while: Pay me your $9 a gallon excise tax and you will get your clearance papers allowing you to land your cargoes in the United States. When he facilitates the entry of - that liquor into United States, gives the smuggler clearance papers and facilitates him in his work, how can he expect the smuggler to respect his request not to smuggle goods back from the United States into Canada? It seems to me that he cannot expect our citizens to respect the laws of this country so long as our government does not respect the laws of the adjoining country.
It has often been brought to my mind very forcibly that the export liquor traffic, especially in the southwestern peninsula of Ontario, which the trade calls the bottle-neck of the trade-and the bottle-neck it really is, because most of the liquor gravitates into that penin-
sula and crosses over the border at Detroit- has a demoralizing effect upon the citizens of that district, so much so that, as I said before, the Border Cities Star thought it its duty to take a hand in the situation and represent the facts as they were with a view to having the border cities cleaned up. That in a measure was accomplished, but to my personal knowledge, from observation of the trucks that ply our highways day iby day in large numbers laden with liquor for export across the Detroit river, and the certain knowledges of all our citizens that that trade is aided and abetted by the government in giving clearances to liquor laden vessels, it is not at all surprising that there has developed in the minds of the citizens in that district a somewhat lax idea of respect for law in general. It has been mj' observation that there have been more hold-ups on the highways, more bank robberies, more hold-ups of gas stations and the like in that territory within the last few years than there have ever been in the history of Ontario before. Only the other day we had a very unfortunate incident upon No. 2 highway down in that district, when an American citizen shot dead a Canadian citizen who attempted to hold up his car. Knowing, as I say, the state of affairs that exists there, the Detroit citizen was not going to take a chance on what might happen. Surely we owe it to ourselves and to our country to see that the morale of our people is kept at a high standard. Instead of condoning the export of liquor to the United States, the trade which is largely concentrated in that area close to the Detroit river having such a detrimental effect upon our citizens, I say that we owe it to ourselves to use every means in our power to try to stop that traffic.
I was somewhat concerned when the Minister of National Revenue gave us the information that when liquor is exported to any country which does not prohibit its importation the exporter is required to furnish a bond of twice the amount of the excise tax, but anyone who desires to export liquor to the United States is required to pay the excise tax in cash because it was not recognized by the department that he could land a cargo within that country. Then the minister made the observation that the excise tax having been paid and clearance granted it was no more of the department's concern or the concern of the government, but that the liquor was then in the same position as free goods, and [DOT] could go anywhere. The minister, in other words, virtually gave us to understand that having received the money and issued clearance papers, he washes his hands of the

Export of Liquor-Mr. Brown
transaction and says: It is nothing to me; do what you will with this stuff. But is that really the case? I do not think it is. There is a situation developing between this country and the United States that will some day alarm us and we shall be forced to sit up and take notice; and it is developing in that southwestern peninsula of Ontario. We cannot go on indefinitely forcing our goods which are contraband within the United Slates upon that country without engendering their ill-will, and some morning we shall perhaps read in the newspapers that some act has been committed which we shall greatly deplore.
This government has considered the question. It has before it the report.of the royal commission and the endonsation of two poirlia-ments. Then why should there be any excuse offered at this time not to carry out the recommendations made by that royal commission and by the committee of the House of Commons? I eay the least we can expect is that the leader of the government and the leader of the opposition should make a pronouncement upon this question. It seems this debate is going to end without the Prime M-inister and the leader of the opposition being concerned enough about the situation to make a .pronouncement to the house. To my mind this is one of the most important questions 'that has come before the house this session, not only because of the investigation made in 1926 and the recommendation which followed it, but because it involves our honour in connection with a neighbouring nation.
Yesterday I listened very attentively to the remarks of the Prime Minister when he introduced the resolution dealing with the [DOT] Geneva protocol. He stressed the fact that we had to rely on the good faith of the contracting parties. That was the fundamental bond of the whole treaty. Surely in connection with the request of the United States in this regard, good faith means a lot in cementing the international good will that has endured for so many years and that I hope will endure in the years to come. I urge upon the government not to let this matter pass without taking action, but to present to the house a solution for the problem by amending ouir law in the manner recommended by the royal commission which investigated the situation in 1926.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to minimize the importance of this subject. Indeed, in my judgment the control of the liquor traffic is one of the mo:jt important subjects that could engage our attention. Neither do I propose to minimize the difficulties that confront us in dealing with-this particular phase of the liquor traffic. It may very well be that those difficulties peculiar to this phase of the traffic are not sufficiently appreciated in all quarters of the country. Indeed, we shall always have difficulties in dealing with the sale of intoxicating liquor so long as we permit its manufacture. It certainly would be an anomaly if, having granted the distilleries the right to manufacture, we began to interfere with the sale of their product. My own personal inclination would be to stop the whole business, and I hope the time 'may come when the country will see that that is the only way in which the liquor traffic can be handled.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: It will be a long time.

maintopic: EXPORT OF LIQUOR TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The millennium may be a
long time in coming. But I am hopeful the time will come when the general sense of the people of Canada will be in favour of going about the eradication of the liquor traffic in a logical way, in such a way that we will not be confronted with these anomalies that arise from time to time.
We approach this particular question from two different standpoints. We have to approach it from the standpoint of our obligations to our friendly neighbours across the line. It has been urged upon us from some quarters that they have done all they can to control this traffic, and that if we would only do the little bit more necessary to complete their work, their problem would be solved. If that were demonstrated to be true, I should have no hesitation, nor do I think this parliament would have any hesitation, in undertaking to do that little bit more. Unfortunately, as I think has been shown this afternoon by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler), there is good reason to believe they have not taken all the steps that they might have taken, and when we are considering the question from the standpoint of our obligations to our neighbours we cannot altogether ignore that feature of the case. If they come to us with the assertion that they have done everything they can to stop this traffic, and demonstrate to us that that is the case, certainly we should not rest satisfied until we had done everything that lies in our power to help them to enforce their own law. Not that the obligation should be thrown upon us to enforce their law, but that we should lend them friendly assistance in that particular. The treaty was entered into with that abject in view, and so far as its
271G

Export o} Liquor-Mr. Brown
terms are concerned, I do not think it can be shown that Canada has not faithfully lived up to them.
Personally I should be very happy to see us go further and enter into a new treaty, if we could help them and ourselves to eliminate this evil. It is true that we might pass a law forbidding the export of liquor, not dealing with it from the standpoint of simply refusing clearance papers, a procedure which might not be as effective as many people seem to think. But I say it is true we might deal with the matter by passing a law absolutely forbidding the export of liquor to the United States. Towards such a law I would be entirely sympathetic, but I would be compelled to concede that tremendous difficulties would confront us when we were called upon to enforce it, especially when we have distilleries situated within a gunshot of the American border.
Let me add what I intended to say at the outset. When I knew that the government had offered the United States every opportunity for their officers to come over to the Canadian side and get full information as to shipments of liquor destined for that country, I was hopeful that the Americans would accept that offer. It seemed to me, whether it would satisfy those who wished for the refusal of clearance papers or not, that such action might be taken as would have all the effect expected from the refusal of clearance papers without any of the consequent difficulties that might result. It is true the Americans have refused that offer. I cannot understand why. It rather confirms me in the thought that perhaps they have -not been dealing with the matter entirely in good faith. I repeat, personally I should be willing and anxious to see Canada take all possible steps to cooperate with the United States in -enforcing that law. But looking at the matter from our own standpoint. I must say that even if the Americans were negligent in the enforcement of their law, from the point of view of a great many people in Canada who feel that total prohibition is the only final solution of the liquor problem, we are -anxious to see the law a success in the United States, and we should put n-o difficulties in the way of their enforcing it. Then, from our own standpoint, wishing to see -their great social experiment a success, I should be still more anxious that we should do everything within our power to curtail the traffic in liquor across the line. On the other hand-, it cannot -be disputed that apart altogether from the question of short-circuiting liquor, which is after all only incidental, the whole wretched business must of necessity have a demoralizing effect upon our own people; and if through any action on the

,part^ of this government in dealing with this particular phase of the situation we could bring about better conditions, certainly I should be only too happy to support any efforts in that direction.
One feature of the situation has been referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) as a third method of dealing with the duties imposed upon this traffic. Undoubtedly it is a new practice that seems to have been necessitated by the peculiar circumstances of the case. The liquor is not intended to go into consumption in Canada, nor can it come under the export laws or regulations that apply to the export of liquor to countries where it may be legally imported. When the minister was speaking I was compelled to do some thinking on that phase of the situation and I may say frankly that, with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, I do not look with any degree of satisfaction on the fact that Canada is reaping a revenue from that particular branch of the traffic. I may say that in regard to the methods of handling liquor in so many provinces of Canada to-day,
I look with a good deal of alarm on the fact that the revenue that is being received from the traffic is making the people just a little less antagonistic to it than they were before.
I know we are confronted with this situation as we were in Manitoba-that we are to consider whether it would be better to take such revenue as comes from the traffic when it is sold at a high price, or to increase the sale by selling at a lower price. Therefore I cannot altogether agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he urges that we should not collect the excise on this liquor in this particular form inasmuch as it tends to increase the profits of the bootlegger. I cannot [DOT] see it in that light. It seems to me that if the government refused to collect the revenue from the sale of the liquor it would enable the distiller to pass the liquor over to the other people that much cheaper; they would make just as much money selling it a little cheaper as they are doing to-day, and the possibility is that the consumption of that liquor would be vastly increased. I cannot look favorably on any resolution that would tend to increase the consumption of liquor. So that for my part at the present time I find myself on the horns of a dilemma, as to whether I should accept the situation, much as I dislike it, of receiving revenue from the sale of liquor, or in the alternative increase the sale of that liquor.. I can however agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre when he takes exception to the policy of increasing the number of distilleries.

We may take it, then, that it is not the policy of the government to increase the number of distilleries. That attitude on the part of the government will certainly secure my endorsation, which will be given all the more heartily if in some measure they can manage to decrease the number.
The unfortunate thing to-day in the liquor situation in Canada is the fact which is also evident in the old country: So many people are acquiring a vested interest in the traffic that it is consolidating itself more than ever before. The financial interest in the traffic is becoming so widespread that the time seems more and more remote when we shall secure from the people of Canada a vote which will abolish the traffic from our midst. That is one feature of the present situation which I dislike-the fact that more and more citizens are securing a financial interest in the traffic. When that is the case we are not likely to take such steps towards its abolition as many people in this country would like to see taken.
Personally I have this to say in regard to the whole question. I know it is true of many people in this country that they want to see Canada do whatever can be done to help a friendly nation to carry out its laws. I do not altogether agree with what the minister said, that the people were not really concerned about our attitude towards a friendly nation, but were only expressing the views they held as prohibitionists. That is not altogether true, although there may be a measure of truth in it, because I feel that a great many of the honest and right-thinking people of Canada do consider it a reproach to the citizens of this country that we should be engaged in a traffic which is abhorrent to the wishes of our friendly neighbours.
